Chapter 1 topics

Ch 1 Structural Organisation in Animals — Animal Tissues

In multicellular animals, cells rarely act alone. Groups of similar cells that perform a common function are organised together into a tissue. Different tissues combine to form organs, organs combine into organ systems, and organ systems together make up the complete organism. Animal tissues are broadly grouped into four fundamental types: Epithelial, Connective, Muscular and Neural.

1. Levels of Structural Organisation

Figure Z1.1: Hierarchy of structural organisation — from a single cell to the complete organism.

The study of tissues is called Histology. Based on origin and function, all animal tissues fall into four fundamental categories, summarised below and detailed in the sections that follow.

Tissue TypePrimary Function
EpithelialCovering & lining of body surfaces, secretion, protection
ConnectiveBinds, supports and connects other tissues/organs
MuscularProduces movement through contraction
NeuralReceives & transmits stimuli; coordination

2. Epithelial Tissue

Epithelial tissue covers the body surface and lines body cavities, ducts and internal organs. Cells are tightly packed with very little intercellular matrix, sit on a basement membrane, and are avascular (get nourishment by diffusion). Classified by cell shape and number of layers:

Figure Z1.2: Major types of epithelial cells classified by shape — squamous, cuboidal, columnar, ciliated columnar and glandular.
Simple Epithelium: Single layer of cells; found where absorption/filtration/secretion occurs — e.g. lining of blood vessels, kidney tubules, gut lining.
Compound Epithelium: Multiple cell layers; provides protection with little role in secretion/absorption — e.g. skin, oesophagus lining.
Glandular Epithelium: Modified for secretion. Exocrine glands (sweat, salivary) secrete via ducts; endocrine glands (thyroid, pituitary) are ductless, secreting hormones directly into blood.
Special Junctions: Epithelial cells are held together by tight junctions (prevent leakage), adhering junctions (mechanical strength) and gap junctions (allow cell-to-cell communication).
Advanced Insight — Molecular Basis of Junctions
  • Tight junctions (zonula occludens): Formed by transmembrane proteins claudins and occludins that fuse the outer leaflets of adjacent cell membranes into a near-continuous seal, forcing molecules to cross the epithelium transcellularly rather than leaking through the paracellular route (critical in gut lining and the blood–brain barrier).
  • Adhering junctions (zonula adherens & desmosomes): Zonula adherens use transmembrane cadherins linked intracellularly to the actin cytoskeleton via catenins; spot desmosomes anchor intermediate filaments (keratin) via desmoplakin, giving tissues like skin and cardiac muscle mechanical resilience against shearing forces.
  • Gap junctions: Clusters of six connexin subunits form a hemichannel (connexon) in one cell that docks with a connexon on the adjacent cell, creating a hydrophilic pore (~1.5 nm) that allows direct passage of ions and small molecules (<1 kDa) — the structural basis of electrical coupling in cardiac and smooth muscle.
Extended Classification You Should Also Know
  • Keratinised vs non-keratinised stratified squamous: Skin epidermis is keratinised (dead, waterproof surface cells packed with keratin); the lining of the oesophagus, mouth and vagina is non-keratinised (living surface cells, kept moist).
  • Pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium: All cells touch the basement membrane but not all reach the free surface, giving a falsely "layered" look under the microscope — lines the trachea and bronchi, its cilia sweep trapped mucus and dust upward (mucociliary escalator).
  • Transitional epithelium: A stretch-adapted compound epithelium lining the urinary bladder, ureters and part of the urethra; cells change shape from cuboidal (empty bladder) to squamous-like (distended bladder) without tearing.
  • Basement membrane, precisely: Not a single membrane but two layers — the basal lamina (secreted by the epithelial cells themselves; contains laminin, type IV collagen) and the reticular lamina (secreted by underlying connective tissue; contains type III reticular fibres) — together they anchor the epithelium and act as a selective filter (e.g. glomerular basement membrane in the kidney).
NEET Exam Traps
  • Do not confuse "simple" (one layer) with "unicellular" — simple epithelium is still made of many cells, just arranged in a single layer.
  • Epithelium is avascular — it never contains blood vessels of its own; oxygen and nutrients diffuse in from the underlying connective tissue capillaries. Only the connective tissue below is vascular.
  • Endocrine glands are ductless and always release secretions (hormones) directly into blood/lymph, never through a duct — a frequently tested distinguishing line from exocrine glands.

3. Connective Tissue

The most abundant and widely distributed tissue — it links, supports and binds other tissues. Unlike epithelium, connective tissue cells are sparsely arranged and embedded in an abundant intercellular matrix, which may be jelly-like, fluid, dense or rigid.

CategoryExamplesKey Feature
Connective tissue proper (loose)Areolar tissue, Adipose tissueFills space inside organs, fat storage
Connective tissue proper (dense)Tendons, LigamentsTendons join muscle to bone; ligaments join bone to bone — both very strong, poorly vascular
Skeletal (supportive)Cartilage, BoneCartilage: smooth, solid matrix (chondrocytes); Bone: hard, calcified matrix (osteocytes)
Fluid connective tissueBloodPlasma matrix carrying RBCs, WBCs & platelets; transports gases, nutrients, wastes
Figure Z1.3: Representative connective tissues — loose areolar tissue, cartilage (chondrocytes in lacunae), and fluid connective tissue (blood).
Advanced Insight — Cells and Fibres of the Matrix
  • Areolar tissue cell population: Contains fibroblasts (secrete the matrix and fibres), macrophages (phagocytic, immune surveillance), mast cells (release histamine and heparin during inflammation/allergy), and occasional plasma cells and lymphocytes. It sits under the skin and between organs, acting as a packing and shock-absorbing tissue.
  • Fibre types: Collagen fibres (white, inelastic, highest tensile strength — main fibre of tendons and dermis), elastic fibres (yellow, made of elastin, can stretch and recoil — abundant in the walls of large arteries and the ligamentum nuchae), and reticular fibres (fine, branching, form the internal supporting framework of the liver, spleen, and lymph nodes).
  • Adipose tissue is a specialised loose connective tissue where fat-storing cells (adipocytes) predominate; humans mainly have white adipose tissue (energy storage, insulation) with a small amount of metabolically active brown adipose tissue (rich in mitochondria, generates heat via non-shivering thermogenesis, more prominent in infants).
  • Cartilage sub-types: Hyaline cartilage (glassy matrix, most common — nose, larynx, trachea rings, articular surfaces), elastic cartilage (contains elastin fibres for flexibility — pinna of the ear, epiglottis), and fibrocartilage (dense collagen bundles for compressive strength — intervertebral discs, pubic symphysis). Chondrocytes sit in small cavities called lacunae within a matrix secreted by the surrounding perichondrium; cartilage itself is avascular and heals slowly.
  • Bone architecture: Compact bone is organised into cylindrical osteons (Haversian systems) — concentric lamellae of calcified matrix around a central Haversian canal carrying blood vessels and nerves, with osteocytes housed in lacunae connected by tiny canaliculi. Osteoblasts deposit new bone matrix, mature into osteocytes once surrounded by matrix, while osteoclasts (multinucleate, derived from monocyte lineage) resorb bone — the two working in constant balance during bone remodelling.
NEET Exam Traps
  • Blood is classified as a connective tissue, not a separate category — because it has a matrix (plasma) with cells suspended in it, and it develops from mesoderm like other connective tissues. This is one of the most commonly tested single-line facts.
  • Tendons connect muscle to bone; ligaments connect bone to bone — a classic swap-the-definitions distractor in MCQs. Ligaments are more elastic than tendons.
  • Cartilage matrix is secreted by chondroblasts/perichondrium and is solid but flexible (contains chondroitin sulphate); bone matrix is hardened by calcium salts (hydroxyapatite) — do not describe cartilage as "calcified."

4. Muscular Tissue

Made of elongated cells called muscle fibres, containing contractile proteins (actin & myosin) that enable movement.

Figure Z1.4: The three types of muscle tissue — skeletal (striated, voluntary), smooth (unstriated, involuntary) and cardiac (branched, involuntary, with intercalated discs).
TypeLocationControlNucleus
SkeletalAttached to bonesVoluntaryMultinucleate, peripheral
SmoothGut wall, blood vessels, irisInvoluntarySingle, central
CardiacHeart wallInvoluntarySingle, central; joined by intercalated discs
Advanced Insight — How a Muscle Fibre Contracts
  • Each skeletal muscle fibre is packed with thread-like myofibrils, each divided into repeating contractile units called sarcomeres — the region between two successive Z-lines. Alternating dark A-bands (thick myosin filaments) and light I-bands (thin actin filaments only) give skeletal and cardiac muscle their striated appearance.
  • Sliding Filament Theory: A nerve impulse triggers release of Ca²⁺ from the sarcoplasmic reticulum; Ca²⁺ binds troponin, shifting tropomyosin away from myosin-binding sites on actin. Myosin heads (using ATP hydrolysis) then bind actin and pull it inward in a repeated "power stroke," sliding thin filaments over thick filaments — this shortens the sarcomere (I-band and H-zone narrow) without the filaments themselves changing length.
  • The triad — one T-tubule flanked by two terminal cisternae of the sarcoplasmic reticulum — is the structure that couples electrical excitation at the cell surface to Ca²⁺ release deep inside the fibre (excitation-contraction coupling).
  • Smooth muscle lacks sarcomeres and troponin; contraction instead relies on Ca²⁺ binding calmodulin, which activates myosin light-chain kinase — this is why smooth muscle contracts more slowly but can sustain tone for long periods with little fatigue.
NEET Exam Trap

During contraction, the A-band length stays constant — only the I-band and H-zone shorten. A common wrong-option in questions describes the A-band as shrinking; remember only the zones made purely of thin (or purely of thick) filament regions change width.

5. Neural Tissue

Made up of highly specialised cells called neurons, designed to receive, conduct and transmit electrical impulses for coordination of body activities. Supporting neuroglial cells protect and nourish neurons.

Figure Z1.5: Structure of a typical neuron — dendrites receive impulses, the cyton (cell body) integrates them, and the myelinated axon conducts the impulse to axon terminals for transmission to the next cell.
Impulse flow: Dendrite → Cell body (Cyton) → Axon → Axon terminal → Synapse → next neuron/effector organ.
Advanced Insight — Conduction & Synaptic Transmission
  • Resting membrane potential (~ −70 mV) is maintained mainly by the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase pump, which exports 3 Na⁺ for every 2 K⁺ imported, combined with the membrane's much higher resting permeability to K⁺. A stimulus that depolarises the membrane past threshold opens voltage-gated Na⁺ channels, triggering an all-or-none action potential.
  • Myelin sheath, laid down by Schwann cells (PNS) or oligodendrocytes (CNS), is interrupted at regular gaps called Nodes of Ranvier. Because ion channels are concentrated at these nodes, the impulse appears to "jump" from node to node — saltatory conduction — making myelinated axons conduct far faster than unmyelinated ones of the same diameter.
  • Synapse types: At a chemical synapse, the arriving impulse opens voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels in the presynaptic terminal, causing synaptic vesicles to fuse with the membrane and release neurotransmitter (e.g. acetylcholine) into the synaptic cleft, which binds receptors on the postsynaptic membrane — transmission here is one-directional and involves a brief synaptic delay. An electrical synapse (via gap junctions) allows near-instantaneous, bidirectional current flow with no chemical intermediary.
  • Neuroglia outnumber neurons in the CNS; besides structural support, astrocytes help form the blood–brain barrier and regulate the neuronal environment, microglia are resident immune cells, and oligodendrocytes/Schwann cells produce myelin.
NEET Exam Trap

Conduction velocity increases with myelination and axon diameter — do not assume all long axons are automatically the fastest; an unmyelinated axon of the same length conducts far more slowly since it depends on continuous (not saltatory) propagation.

Chapter 2 topics

Ch 2 Biomolecules

Every living cell is a self-contained chemical factory. If you analyse the chemical composition of a cell, you will find both inorganic constituents (water, mineral ions, gases) and organic constituents — the true biomolecules: carbohydrates, proteins, lipids and nucleic acids. This chapter looks at the structure, classification and biological role of each class, and how small building-block molecules polymerise into the giant macromolecules of life. Biomolecular analysis is the foundation of biochemistry, and questions from this chapter appear almost every year in NEET — usually testing exact numbers (bond angles, number of H-bonds, number of amino acids), classic exceptions, and NCERT-line definitions, so precision matters more than in most other chapters.

Big picture: All four major biomolecule classes follow the same architectural logic — a small, repeating monomer unit is joined to identical or similar units by a specific covalent bond, releasing a water molecule each time (dehydration/condensation). The reverse reaction — hydrolysis — adds water back and breaks the polymer down, which is exactly what digestive enzymes do. Keep this monomer → bond → polymer → hydrolysis framework in mind for every section below.

1. Chemical Composition of the Cell

If you take a tissue, grind it in trichloroacetic acid (TCA) and filter it, you get an acid-soluble pool (small molecules — amino acids, sugars, nucleotides, etc.) and a filter residue made of larger macromolecules (proteins, nucleic acids, polysaccharides, lipids). Elemental analysis shows carbon, hydrogen, oxygen and nitrogen make up the bulk of dry weight, with smaller amounts of phosphorus, sulphur and trace elements.

Any substance found in the acid-soluble pool is called a micromolecule or metabolite. Metabolites are divided by function: amino acids (building blocks of proteins), monosaccharides & disaccharides (simple sugars), fatty acids & glycerol (lipid components), nitrogenous bases, and other small compounds like vitamins and various acids/gases dissolved in the cell (CO₂, N₂). Some metabolites take part directly in metabolic reactions; others (secondary metabolites such as alkaloids, terpenoids, essential oils, gums, antibiotics, and pigments) have no obvious role in normal physiology but are of great commercial and pharmaceutical importance — e.g. vinblastine, curcumin, morphine, strychnine, and rubber.

Quantitatively, if you determine the "wet weight" of a tissue and remove all the water, the remaining dry weight is made up overwhelmingly of carbon compounds. Elemental analysis of a living cell (percentage on a dry-weight basis, approximate) typically shows: Oxygen > Carbon > Hydrogen > Nitrogen, together accounting for >90% of dry weight, with phosphorus, sulphur, calcium, potassium, sodium, chlorine, magnesium, iron and trace elements (Mn, Cu, Zn, I, Mo, etc.) making up the rest — the same elements found in non-living matter, which is why the elemental composition of living and non-living matter is qualitatively identical (a key NEET-line fact used to argue that no "vital force" separates biochemistry from ordinary chemistry).

Figure Z2.1: Separating a cell's chemical constituents into the acid-soluble pool of micromolecules and the macromolecule-rich filter residue.
Biomolecule ClassBuilding Block (Monomer)Bond Linking Monomers
Carbohydrates (polysaccharides)MonosaccharidesGlycosidic bond
ProteinsAmino acidsPeptide bond
Nucleic AcidsNucleotidesPhosphodiester bond
LipidsGlycerol + fatty acidsEster bond
NEET point: Water is the most abundant chemical in any living tissue (60–90%), acting as an excellent solvent and medium for metabolic reactions.

Micromolecules vs macromolecules: Macromolecules of the acid-insoluble fraction have a much higher molecular weight (in the thousands to millions of daltons) than micromolecules (typically under 1000 Da), and unlike micromolecules they are heterogeneous — a protein's exact chemical identity depends on the precise sequence of its monomers, not just the ratio of atoms. This is why a template-based synthesis mechanism (transcription/translation, or DNA replication) is essential for building macromolecules like proteins and nucleic acids, but not for simple metabolites.

Dynamic State of Body Constituents: Although the concentration of each metabolite in a cell (its steady state) stays remarkably constant, the actual molecules are being continuously synthesised and broken down — this is the concept of metabolic flux. Every chemical reaction occurring inside a living organism, whether it builds up molecules (anabolism, e.g. photosynthesis, protein synthesis) or breaks them down (catabolism, e.g. respiration, digestion), is collectively called metabolism. Metabolism is characteristic only of the living state — no chemical reaction inside a living cell occurs in isolation from every other reaction, which is why cells maintain a "structural organisation" of enzymes rather than metabolites simply reacting at random, as they would in a beaker.

Common qualitative tests (frequently asked):

TestDetectsPositive Result
Molisch's testCarbohydrates (general)Violet/purple ring at the interface
Benedict's / Fehling's testReducing sugarsBrick-red precipitate (Cu₂O)
Iodine testStarchBlue-black colour
Biuret testProteins / peptide bondsViolet/purple colour
Sudan III / Sudan IV testLipidsRed/orange colouration of fat globules
Xanthoproteic testAromatic amino acids in proteinsYellow colour with conc. HNO₃

2. Carbohydrates

Carbohydrates are polyhydroxy aldehydes or ketones (general formula roughly (CH₂O)ₙ, though this ratio isn't exact for all sugars — e.g. deoxyribose, C₅H₁₀O₄, doesn't fit it), the chief source of energy and important structural components. Based on the aldehyde (–CHO) or ketone (C=O) group present, monosaccharides are further classed as aldoses (glucose, ribose) or ketoses (fructose), and by carbon number as trioses (3C), tetroses (4C), pentoses (5C, e.g. ribose, deoxyribose — found in nucleic acids), hexoses (6C, e.g. glucose, fructose, galactose) and so on. Based on the number of sugar units, they are classified into three groups:

Figure Z2.2: Classification of carbohydrates by chain length — monosaccharides join via glycosidic bonds to form oligosaccharides and, ultimately, long-chain polysaccharides.

A glycosidic bond forms between two monosaccharides by loss of a water molecule (condensation/dehydration reaction) — e.g. glucose + glucose → maltose. Polysaccharides can be homopolysaccharides (one type of monomer, e.g. starch, cellulose — both made only of glucose) or heteropolysaccharides (more than one type of monomer).

PolysaccharideFound InFunction
StarchPlants (amylose + amylopectin)Storage form of glucose
GlycogenAnimals, fungi (liver, muscle)Storage form of glucose in animals
CellulosePlant cell wallsStructural — unbranched glucose chain
ChitinInsect exoskeleton, fungal cell wallStructural polysaccharide of N-acetylglucosamine
NEET point: Starch gives a blue-black colour with iodine; it's a branched (amylopectin) + unbranched (amylose) glucose polymer, unlike cellulose which is a straight, unbranched chain.

Reducing vs non-reducing sugars: A sugar is reducing if it has a free aldehyde or ketone group that can reduce Cu²⁺ (Benedict's/Fehling's reagent) to Cu⁺ (brick-red Cu₂O). All monosaccharides (glucose, fructose, galactose) and most disaccharides (maltose, lactose) are reducing sugars. Sucrose is the classic exception — its glycosidic bond links the anomeric (reducing) carbons of both glucose and fructose, leaving no free reducing group, so it is non-reducing. In solution, monosaccharides like glucose mostly exist as a cyclic ring (pyranose, 6-membered, or furanose, 5-membered) formed when the carbonyl carbon reacts with a hydroxyl group elsewhere in the same molecule, generating a new stereocentre — the anomeric carbon — that gives rise to α- and β-anomers.

Structural polysaccharides & mucopolysaccharides: Besides starch, glycogen, cellulose and chitin, NEET occasionally tests mucopolysaccharides/glycosaminoglycans — heteropolysaccharides such as hyaluronic acid and chondroitin sulphate found in the extracellular matrix and connective tissue (ground substance). Glycogen is more highly branched than amylopectin, which lets liver and muscle cells mobilise glucose faster during high energy demand. Inulin (a fructose polymer, storage carbohydrate of some plants like dahlia) is another commonly asked exception to the "glucose-only" rule for storage polysaccharides.

3. Proteins

Proteins are polymers of amino acids linked by peptide bonds. Every amino acid has a central (α) carbon bonded to an amino group (–NH₂), a carboxyl group (–COOH), a hydrogen atom, and a variable side chain (R group) that gives each of the 20 amino acids its distinct identity.

Figure Z2.3: General structure of an amino acid, and formation of a peptide bond between two amino acids by loss of a water molecule (dehydration/condensation).

Amino acids are grouped as essential (cannot be synthesised by the body, must come from diet, e.g. valine, leucine, isoleucine, lysine, methionine, phenylalanine, threonine, tryptophan, histidine) and non-essential (body can synthesise them, e.g. glycine, alanine). A chain of amino acids joined by peptide bonds is a polypeptide; a functional protein may consist of one or more polypeptide chains folded into a specific 3-D shape. Because an amino acid carries both an ionisable –NH₂ (basic) and –COOH (acidic) group, it behaves as an amphoteric/zwitterion in solution (simultaneously carrying a positive and a negative charge), and each amino acid has a characteristic isoelectric point (pI) — the pH at which its net charge is zero. Based on the R group, amino acids are also classified as acidic (e.g. glutamic acid, aspartic acid), basic (e.g. lysine, arginine, histidine) or neutral, and as polar or non-polar — this classification underlies protein folding, since non-polar side chains bury themselves away from water in the protein's hydrophobic core.

Figure Z2.4: Four levels of protein structure — from the linear amino acid sequence (primary) to multi-subunit assemblies (quaternary), e.g. haemoglobin's four polypeptide chains.
NEET point: Collagen (most abundant protein in animals) and trypsin are common NEET examples. Haemoglobin shows quaternary structure with 2 α- and 2 β-globin chains.

Four levels of protein structure, in detail:

LevelDescriptionStabilising Interaction
PrimaryLinear sequence of amino acids joined by peptide bonds — determines everything above itCovalent peptide bonds
SecondaryLocal, regular folding pattern — α-helix (coiled, right-handed) or β-pleated sheet (extended, zig-zag strands)Hydrogen bonds between backbone C=O and N–H groups
TertiaryOverall 3-D folding of a single polypeptide into a compact globular or fibrous shapeHydrophobic interactions, hydrogen bonds, ionic bonds, disulphide (–S–S–) bridges
QuaternaryArrangement of two or more polypeptide subunits into one functional protein (only in multi-subunit proteins)Same non-covalent forces as tertiary structure, between subunits

Classification by shape: Fibrous proteins (e.g. collagen, keratin) have elongated, thread-like polypeptide chains lying parallel along an axis and are structurally supportive/insoluble in water; globular proteins (e.g. most enzymes, haemoglobin, insulin, antibodies) have chains folded into a compact, roughly spherical shape and are usually water-soluble and functionally active (transport, catalysis, defence). Proteins that also contain a non-protein (prosthetic) group are called conjugated proteins — e.g. haemoglobin (a chromoprotein, with a haem/iron group), glycoproteins (carbohydrate group), and lipoproteins (lipid group).

Denaturation: When a protein is exposed to physical (heat, high pressure) or chemical (extreme pH, heavy metals, organic solvents) stress, its non-covalent secondary/tertiary/quaternary interactions are disrupted and it loses its native 3-D shape and biological activity — the primary structure (peptide bonds) usually remains intact. A classic example is albumin in raw egg white coagulating into a rubbery solid on boiling. Denaturation is generally irreversible.

4. Lipids

Lipids are generally water-insoluble (hydrophobic), often containing fatty acids. A fatty acid has a carboxyl group attached to an R group that can be a methyl (–CH₃), ethyl, or a longer hydrocarbon chain. If the hydrocarbon chain has no double bonds, it is a saturated fatty acid; with one or more double bonds, it is unsaturated.

Figure Z2.5: A triglyceride is formed by esterification of glycerol with three fatty acid molecules.
Lipid TypeCompositionExample / Role
Simple lipids (fats/oils)Glycerol + fatty acidsEnergy storage (adipose tissue)
PhospholipidsGlycerol + 2 fatty acids + phosphate groupMajor component of cell membranes (e.g. lecithin)
SteroidsFused ring structure, no fatty acidsCholesterol, sex hormones
WaxesLong chain fatty acid + long chain alcoholWaterproof coatings (skin, cuticle)
NEET point: Ghee/butter are saturated fats (solid at room temperature); groundnut/til oil are unsaturated fats (liquid at room temperature).

Essential fatty acids: Fatty acids the human body cannot synthesise and must obtain from the diet — mainly linoleic acid (omega-6) and linolenic acid (omega-3) — are called essential fatty acids; they are needed for membrane structure and as precursors of signalling molecules (e.g. prostaglandins). "Omega" numbering refers to the position of the first double bond counted from the methyl (–CH₃) end of the chain.

Phospholipids & membrane structure: A phospholipid molecule is amphipathic — it has a hydrophilic (water-loving) phosphate "head" and two hydrophobic (water-fearing) fatty-acid "tails." In water, phospholipids spontaneously arrange into a bilayer with tails facing inward, away from water, and heads facing outward — this self-assembling bilayer is the structural basis of every cell membrane (Singer & Nicolson's fluid mosaic model). Emulsification is the process (aided by bile salts in digestion) by which large fat globules are broken into smaller droplets to increase surface area for lipase action.

Steroids are lipids built on a fused four-ring carbon skeleton rather than fatty-acid chains; cholesterol is the most important animal steroid — a component of cell membranes and the precursor for steroid hormones (testosterone, oestrogen, cortisol) and bile acids. Because steroids and fats/oils are both hydrophobic they are grouped together as lipids even though their chemical structures are very different — a commonly tested NCERT distinction.

5. Nucleic Acids

Nucleic acids (DNA and RNA) are polymers of nucleotides. Each nucleotide has three components: a nitrogenous base, a pentose sugar, and a phosphate group. A base + sugar alone (without phosphate) is called a nucleoside — the base attaches to the sugar's 1′ carbon by an N-glycosidic bond, and phosphate attaches at the 5′ (and sometimes 3′) carbon by an ester bond; together these two links make up the phosphodiester bond that connects one nucleotide's 5′-phosphate to the next nucleotide's 3′-OH, giving the polynucleotide chain a fixed chemical direction (5′ → 3′).

Figure Z2.6: Structure of a single nucleotide, and how successive nucleotides link via phosphodiester bonds to build a polynucleotide chain.

Nitrogenous bases are of two types: purines (double-ring — Adenine, Guanine) and pyrimidines (single-ring — Cytosine, Thymine, Uracil). In the DNA double helix, bases pair specifically: A = T (2 hydrogen bonds) and G ≡ C (3 hydrogen bonds) — this is complementary base pairing. The two polynucleotide strands run antiparallel to each other, as established by Watson and Crick (1953).

FeatureDNARNA
SugarDeoxyriboseRibose
Pyrimidine baseThymine (T)Uracil (U) instead of Thymine
StrandsDouble-stranded helixUsually single-stranded
FunctionStores genetic informationmRNA, tRNA, rRNA — protein synthesis
NEET point: Adenine always pairs with Thymine (or Uracil in RNA); Guanine always pairs with Cytosine — remember "Purine pairs with Pyrimidine" to keep helix width constant.

B-DNA geometry (Watson–Crick model, numbers NEET loves to ask): a right-handed double helix with a diameter of about 20 Å; one complete turn spans 3.4 nm (34 Å) and contains 10 base pairs, so successive base pairs are 0.34 nm apart; the two strands are held together by hydrogen bonds between paired bases and by base-stacking interactions, and the helix has a major groove and a minor groove where regulatory proteins bind. Inside living cells, DNA is normally negatively supercoiled and packaged with basic proteins called histones — a length of DNA wound around a histone octamer forms a nucleosome, the basic repeating unit of chromatin ("beads-on-a-string").

Three types of RNA and their roles (all single-stranded, though they can fold back on themselves to form local double-helical/hairpin regions):

RNA TypeFull NameFunction
mRNAmessenger RNACarries the genetic code from DNA to ribosomes as a template for protein synthesis
tRNAtransfer RNASmallest RNA; clover-leaf shape; reads the codon and carries the corresponding amino acid to the ribosome
rRNAribosomal RNAStructural and catalytic component of ribosomes; most abundant RNA in the cell

Note the key exception for exam purposes: certain viruses (e.g. some plant viruses like TMV, and many animal viruses) use RNA, not DNA, as their genetic material, and it can even be double-stranded (e.g. reoviruses) — so "DNA = genetic material" is the rule, but not an absolute one.

6. Enzymes

Enzymes are (mostly) proteins that act as biocatalysts — they speed up biochemical reactions without being consumed, by lowering the activation energy needed for a reaction to proceed. (A few catalytic RNA molecules, called ribozymes, are the notable non-protein exception.) Each enzyme has a specific 3-D pocket called the active site where the substrate binds; this specificity is explained by two historical models — the rigid "lock-and-key" model (Emil Fischer) and the more accurate induced-fit model, where the active site actually changes shape slightly as the substrate binds, improving the fit.

Figure Z2.7: Enzyme action (induced fit model) — the substrate binds the active site, forms an enzyme-substrate complex, reaction occurs, and the unchanged enzyme is released along with the product.

Enzyme activity is affected by temperature and pH — each enzyme has an optimum temperature/pH range for maximum activity, beyond which the protein denatures and activity falls. Enzymes are classified into six major classes based on the reaction they catalyse:

ClassType of Reaction Catalysed
OxidoreductasesOxidation-reduction between two substrates
TransferasesTransfer of a group between substrates
HydrolasesHydrolysis (transfer of group to water)
LyasesRemoval of a group to form a double bond
IsomerasesRearrangement within a molecule (isomer formation)
LigasesJoining two molecules using ATP energy

Cofactors — non-protein "helpers": Many enzymes need a non-protein component to function. Three types are recognised: (1) prosthetic groups — organic molecules tightly/permanently bound to the enzyme (e.g. haem in catalase); (2) co-enzymes — organic molecules that bind loosely and transiently, often vitamin-derived (e.g. NAD⁺, NADP⁺, FAD, coenzyme A); (3) metal ions/cofactors — inorganic ions that form coordination bonds at the active site (e.g. Zn²⁺ in carboxypeptidase). The protein part of an enzyme without its cofactor is called the apoenzyme; apoenzyme + cofactor together = the active holoenzyme.

Enzyme kinetics (Michaelis–Menten): As substrate concentration [S] increases at a fixed enzyme concentration, reaction velocity rises and gradually plateaus at a maximum velocity, Vmax, once every enzyme molecule's active site is saturated with substrate. The substrate concentration at which velocity is exactly half of Vmax is called the Michaelis constant, Km — a lower Km indicates higher enzyme–substrate affinity (less substrate needed to reach half-maximal velocity).

Enzyme inhibition: A competitive inhibitor has a shape similar to the natural substrate and competes for the same active site — its effect can be overcome by adding more substrate (classic example: malonate competitively inhibiting succinate dehydrogenase). A non-competitive inhibitor binds elsewhere on the enzyme (an allosteric site), changing the enzyme's shape and reducing activity regardless of substrate concentration — this cannot be reversed simply by adding more substrate.

Allosteric regulation & feedback inhibition: Many enzymes have, in addition to the active site, a separate allosteric site where a regulatory (allosteric) molecule binds and changes the enzyme's activity/shape — this is a key mechanism for regulating metabolic pathways. In feedback (end-product) inhibition, the final product of a metabolic pathway accumulates and binds allosterically to an early enzyme in that same pathway, switching it off — an elegant, self-limiting control loop that prevents wasteful overproduction.

Factors affecting enzyme activity: besides temperature and pH (each enzyme shows a bell-shaped activity curve with a distinct optimum — most human enzymes work best near 37°C and near-neutral pH, though pepsin is a well-known exception that works best around pH 2), activity also depends on substrate concentration and enzyme concentration.

Chapter 3 topics

Ch 3 Breathing and Exchange of Gases

Every living cell needs a continuous supply of O₂ to oxidise food and release energy, and must get rid of the CO₂ produced. Breathing (respiration in the physical sense) is the mechanical process of taking in atmospheric air rich in O₂ and giving out CO₂-rich alveolar air. The energy-releasing biochemical process inside cells is cellular respiration — a separate topic. This chapter covers respiratory organs, the human respiratory system, breathing mechanics, gas exchange/transport, and their regulation.

1. Respiratory Organs Across the Animal Kingdom

Different animal groups use different respiratory structures depending on habitat and complexity:

Animal GroupRespiratory Organ
Lower invertebrates (Protozoans, sponges, coelenterates)General body surface (diffusion)
Earthworm (Annelids)Moist cuticle (skin)
InsectsTracheal tubes (network opening via spiracles)
Fish, PrawnsGills
AmphibiansMoist skin + Lungs (dual respiration)
Reptiles, Birds, MammalsLungs
NEET point: In insects, tracheal tubes carry O₂ directly to tissues — the blood (haemolymph) plays no role in O₂ transport in insects, unlike in vertebrates.

2. Human Respiratory System

Air enters through the external nares (nostrils) → nasal chamber (lined with mucus + hair to filter dust and warm/moisten air) → pharynx → larynx (voice box, contains vocal cords) → trachea (windpipe, supported by C-shaped cartilage rings that prevent collapse) → primary bronchi (one to each lung) → bronchioles → alveoli (site of gas exchange).

Figure Z3.1: Human respiratory pathway — nasal chamber → pharynx → larynx → trachea → bronchi → lungs (bronchioles and alveoli).

Each lung is covered by a double-layered membrane, the pleura — the outer parietal pleura (attached to the thoracic wall) and the inner visceral pleura (attached to the lung surface), with pleural fluid between them reducing friction.

3. Mechanism of Breathing

Breathing involves two stages — inspiration (air moves in) and expiration (air moves out) — driven purely by pressure/volume changes in the thoracic cavity, following Boyle's Law (P ∝ 1/V at constant temperature). Lungs have no muscles of their own; they are elastic, stretchable sacs that passively follow whatever the thoracic cage does — so the whole mechanism really is about changing thoracic volume first, with the lungs and the air inside following along. Two pressures matter here: intrapulmonary (intra-alveolar) pressure, the pressure inside the alveoli, and intrapleural pressure, the pressure in the thin fluid-filled space between the two pleural layers, which stays slightly negative (sub-atmospheric) throughout the cycle and is what keeps the lungs from collapsing under their own elastic recoil.

Inspiration mechanics: The diaphragm (dome-shaped muscle) contracts and flattens, while the external intercostal muscles contract, lifting the ribs and sternum outward and upward. Both actions enlarge the thoracic cavity in the vertical and antero-posterior/transverse directions simultaneously. As the thorax expands, the pleural cavity is dragged along with it, so intrapleural pressure drops even further below atmospheric. The lungs, being elastic, are stretched by this and their volume increases, which by Boyle's Law drops intrapulmonary pressure below atmospheric pressure (roughly −1 to −3 mmHg relative to atmosphere at rest). Air rushes in down this pressure gradient until intrapulmonary pressure re-equals atmospheric pressure — that is what stops inspiration, not the lungs "filling up."

Expiration mechanics: The diaphragm relaxes and domes back upward into the thorax; the external intercostals relax and the ribs swing back down and in, largely under elastic recoil of the costal cartilages and lung tissue itself (very little active muscle work at rest — this is why quiet expiration is called passive). Thoracic volume falls, intrapulmonary pressure rises above atmospheric (roughly +1 to +3 mmHg), and air flows out until pressures re-equalise. During forced/deep expiration (coughing, sneezing, blowing out candles), the internal intercostal muscles actively pull the ribs further down and in, and the abdominal muscles contract to push the diaphragm further up, expelling air beyond the passive amount.

Figure Z3.2: During inspiration the diaphragm contracts and the ribs move outward, increasing thoracic volume and drawing air in; expiration reverses these changes, pushing air out.

Inspiration is normally active (needs muscle contraction — diaphragm + external intercostal muscles); quiet expiration is largely passive (elastic recoil of lungs and relaxation of muscles), though forced expiration involves internal intercostals and abdominal muscles.

NEET exam traps:
  • Direction of diaphragm movement is a classic flip trap — it flattens/moves down during inspiration and domes upward during expiration; questions often reverse this.
  • Do not confuse intrapulmonary pressure (fluctuates above/below atmospheric each cycle, and equals atmospheric at the very end of both inspiration and expiration) with intrapleural pressure (always remains negative relative to atmospheric, even at the end of expiration — never becomes positive in normal quiet breathing).
  • External intercostals → inspiration (ribs up and out); internal intercostals → forced expiration (ribs down and in) — these two muscle sets are frequently swapped in MCQs.
  • NCERT numeric values to memorise directly: normal person breathes in/out ~500 mL of air (tidal volume) in a single normal breath, and can inspire/expire ~6000–8000 mL of air per minute (12–16 breaths/min).

4. Respiratory Volumes and Capacities

A spirometer measures the volume of air a person inhales/exhales, helping assess pulmonary function. Approximate values for a healthy human adult:

TermDefinitionApprox. Value
Tidal Volume (TV)Air breathed in/out in normal (quiet) respiration~500 mL
Inspiratory Reserve Volume (IRV)Extra air inhaled by forcible inspiration beyond TV~2500–3000 mL
Expiratory Reserve Volume (ERV)Extra air exhaled by forcible expiration beyond TV~1000–1100 mL
Residual Volume (RV)Air remaining in lungs even after forcible expiration~1100–1200 mL
Vital Capacity (VC = TV+IRV+ERV)Maximum air a person can breathe out after forced inspiration~3700–4600 mL
Total Lung Capacity (TLC = VC+RV)Total air volume the lungs can hold~4500–6000 mL
NEET point: A person breathes in/out ~6000–8000 mL of air per minute at rest (12–16 breaths × 500 mL tidal volume).

5. Exchange and Transport of Gases

Gas exchange happens by simple diffusion — no active transport or ATP is used at this step — driven by the partial pressure gradient (pO₂ and pCO₂) between alveoli, blood and tissues, across a very thin alveolar-capillary membrane. There are two such exchange sites: alveoli ↔ pulmonary blood (external/pulmonary respiration) and blood ↔ tissues (internal respiration). The rate of diffusion at each site depends on several factors (essentially Fick's Law of diffusion): the pressure gradient of the gas, the solubility of the gas in the membrane/fluid (CO₂ is about 20–25× more soluble in the membrane than O₂, which is why CO₂ diffuses efficiently even though its pressure gradient is much smaller than O₂'s), the thickness of the membrane (thickening — e.g. in fibrosis — slows diffusion), and the total surface area available (millions of alveoli give the human lung an enormous surface area, roughly 70–80 m², for exchange).

Figure Z3.3: O₂ diffuses down its pressure gradient from alveoli → blood → tissues, while CO₂ diffuses the opposite way, from tissues → blood → alveoli.

O₂ transport: ~97% is carried by haemoglobin (Hb) as oxyhaemoglobin — each Hb molecule has 4 haem groups and can bind up to 4 O₂ molecules; only ~3% dissolves directly in plasma (plasma is a poor solvent for O₂). Binding of O₂ to Hb is cooperative: binding of the first O₂ makes it easier for the next to bind, which is why the graph of % saturation of Hb with O₂ against pO₂ — the oxygen dissociation curve (ODC) — is sigmoid (S-shaped), not a straight line or a simple hyperbola. At the alveoli (high pO₂ ≈ 104 mmHg, low pCO₂, higher pH, lower temperature), the curve favours O₂ loading onto Hb; at the tissues (low pO₂ ≈ 40 mmHg, high pCO₂, lower pH, higher temperature), it favours O₂ unloading from Hb. A rise in pCO₂, H⁺ concentration (fall in pH) and temperature all shift the ODC to the right, lowering Hb's affinity for O₂ and promoting unloading in active, CO₂-producing, warmer tissue — this is the Bohr effect, and it is what lets exercising muscle pull extra O₂ off Hb exactly where it's needed most.

CO₂ transport: ~70% travels as bicarbonate (HCO₃⁻). CO₂ diffuses into RBCs, where the enzyme carbonic anhydrase rapidly catalyses CO₂ + H₂O ⇌ H₂CO₃ ⇌ H⁺ + HCO₃⁻. The HCO₃⁻ formed diffuses out into the plasma for transport (in exchange for Cl⁻ moving into the RBC to maintain electrical neutrality — the chloride shift), while the H⁺ released is buffered mainly by binding to deoxygenated Hb inside the cell. ~20–25% is carried as carbamino-haemoglobin (CO₂ bound directly to the globin part of Hb, not the haem, so it doesn't compete with O₂ binding at the same site), and only ~7% dissolves directly in plasma. At the tissues, deoxygenated Hb binds CO₂ and H⁺ more readily than oxygenated Hb does, which promotes CO₂ loading into blood — the reverse process, where oxygenation of Hb in the lungs promotes release of CO₂ and H⁺ from Hb, is called the Haldane effect. Bohr and Haldane effects are essentially two sides of the same allosteric coin: each gas's binding to Hb is enhanced by the absence, and reduced by the presence, of the other.

NEET exam traps:
  • Don't mix up the Bohr effect (CO₂/H⁺/temperature promoting O₂ unloading from Hb) with the Haldane effect (O₂ promoting CO₂/H⁺ unloading from Hb) — they are reciprocal, not identical.
  • Memorise the CO₂ transport split exactly as NCERT gives it: ~70% as bicarbonate, ~20–25% as carbaminohaemoglobin, ~7% dissolved in plasma — questions often swap the 70% and 20–25% figures.
  • Carbonic anhydrase is concentrated in RBCs, not plasma — this is why the bicarbonate reaction happens fast only after CO₂ enters the erythrocyte.
  • The ODC is sigmoid because of cooperative binding across 4 haem sites — a common distractor calls it a "rectangular hyperbola," which is actually the shape for myoglobin (a single-haem protein with no cooperativity), not haemoglobin.

6. Regulation of Respiration & Disorders

Breathing is regulated by the nervous system to keep pace with the body's demands. The main respiratory rhythm centre is in the medulla oblongata, which continuously generates the rhythm of inspiration/expiration. The pneumotaxic centre in the pons can moderate the medulla's rhythm and reduce inspiration duration. A chemosensitive area adjacent to the rhythm centre is highly sensitive to CO₂ and H⁺ ions — a rise in these strongly stimulates the centre for corrective action, making CO₂ (not O₂) the primary respiratory stimulus.

DisorderDescription
AsthmaDifficulty in breathing due to inflammation/spasm of bronchi and bronchioles
EmphysemaChronic disorder — alveolar walls damaged (often by smoking), reducing surface area for gas exchange
Occupational respiratory disordersCaused by long-term exposure to dust (e.g. silicosis in stone/mining workers) causing fibrosis
NEET point: The chemosensitive area is far more sensitive to CO₂/H⁺ than O₂ — this is why CO₂ level, not O₂ level, is the main driver of respiratory rate.
Chapter 4 topics

Ch 4 Body Fluids and Circulation

Multicellular animals need an efficient transport system to carry O₂, nutrients, hormones, wastes and heat to and from every cell — simple diffusion is far too slow to serve cells lying deep inside a large body. In humans this job is done by two body fluids — blood and lymph — driven around the body by a muscular pump, the heart, working within a closed system of vessels. This chapter covers blood composition, plasma proteins, blood groups, the clotting cascade, lymph and the lymphatic system, heart structure and conduction, the cardiac cycle with ECG, and double circulation with its regulation and disorders — all high-yield NEET areas.

1. Composition of Blood

Blood is a special fluid connective tissue with a liquid matrix (plasma) and formed elements (cells) suspended in it. An adult human has roughly 5–5.5 litres of blood, about 8% of body weight, with plasma pH maintained close to 7.4.

Figure Z4.1: Blood composition — a fluid plasma matrix carrying proteins/ions/nutrients, plus formed cellular elements (RBCs, WBCs, platelets).

(a) Plasma is a straw-coloured, viscous fluid — about 90–92% water, with 6–8% proteins, and the rest small amounts of glucose, amino acids, lipids, hormones and electrolytes (Na⁺, Ca²⁺, K⁺, HCO₃⁻ etc.) that help maintain osmotic balance. Plasma without the clotting factors/fibrinogen is called serum.

Plasma ProteinMade ByMain Function
AlbuminsLiverMaintain osmotic (oncotic) pressure and blood volume
GlobulinsLiver & lymphoid tissueImmunoglobulins (antibodies) fight infection; also transport lipids/hormones
FibrinogenLiverPrecursor of fibrin — essential for blood clotting

(b) Formed elements (~45% of blood by volume, expressed as haematocrit/PCV):

Formed ElementKey FeatureNormal CountFunction
RBC (Erythrocytes)Biconcave disc, anucleate & no mitochondria in mammals; ~120-day lifespan; formed by erythropoiesis in red bone marrow (liver/spleen in foetus); destroyed in spleen ("graveyard of RBCs")5–5.5 million /mm³ (males slightly higher than females)Haemoglobin (Hb, ~12–16 g/100 mL blood) carries O₂ & some CO₂
WBC (Leucocytes)Nucleated, colourless; 5 types — granulocytes (neutrophils, eosinophils, basophils) & agranulocytes (monocytes, lymphocytes)6,000–8,000 /mm³Immunity / defence against pathogens
Platelets (Thrombocytes)Small, enucleate cell fragments pinched off from megakaryocytes (bone marrow)1.5–3.5 lakh /mm³Release factors essential for blood clotting

WBC differential count (relative abundance and role of each type):

WBC Type% of WBCsNucleus / GranulesFunction
Neutrophils60–65% (most abundant)Multi-lobed; faintly stained granulesPhagocytose bacteria/pathogens ("first responders")
Lymphocytes20–25%Large single nucleus; agranulocyteB-lymphocytes → antibodies (humoral immunity); T-lymphocytes → cell-mediated immunity
Monocytes6–8%Kidney/bean-shaped nucleus; agranulocyteEnter tissues, mature into macrophages — phagocytosis
Eosinophils2–3%Bilobed nucleus; large acidophilic granulesResist infections, active in allergic reactions & anti-parasitic response
Basophils0.5–1% (least abundant)Granules stain with basic dyesRelease histamin, serotonin, heparin — inflammatory & allergic responses
NEET point: Mnemonic for decreasing WBC abundance — "Never Let Monkeys Eat Bananas" = Neutrophils > Lymphocytes > Monocytes > Eosinophils > Basophils. Also remember: RBCs are anucleate and lack mitochondria (they rely on anaerobic glycolysis), so they cannot divide and are continuously replaced from bone marrow stem cells. A rise in eosinophil count often signals allergy or parasitic (e.g. helminth) infection — a favourite assertion-reason question.

2. Blood Groups and Blood Clotting

The ABO blood group system is based on the presence/absence of surface antigens (A, B) on RBCs, and corresponding antibodies in plasma:

Blood GroupAntigen on RBCAntibody in Plasma
AAAnti-B
BBAnti-A
ABA and BNone — universal recipient
ONone — universal donorAnti-A and Anti-B

The ABO groups are determined by a single gene with three alleles — IA, IB and i — of which IA and IB are co-dominant and both are dominant over i. This is a classic NEET genetics crossover topic: genotype IAIA or IAi gives blood group A; IBIB or IBi gives group B; IAIB gives group AB; and ii gives group O.

Before transfusion, matching is essential — mixing incompatible blood causes the donor RBCs to clump/agglutinate when they meet the matching antibody in the recipient's plasma. Group O is the "universal donor" (no antigens to react with recipient antibodies) and AB is the "universal recipient" (no antibodies to react with donor antigens), though in practice same-group transfusion is always preferred.

The Rh factor (named after the Rhesus monkey, in which it was first discovered) is another RBC surface antigen; Rh⁺ individuals have it, Rh⁻ individuals don't — about 80% of humans are Rh⁺. Rh incompatibility between an Rh⁻ mother and Rh⁺ foetus (father Rh⁺) is clinically important: during the first pregnancy, foetal RBCs normally don't cross the placenta and the mother stays unsensitised, but during delivery some leakage can occur, sensitising the mother's immune system to produce anti-Rh antibodies. If she carries a Rh⁺ foetus again, these antibodies can cross the placenta and destroy foetal RBCs, causing erythroblastosis foetalis (Haemolytic Disease of the Newborn). This is preventable by giving the Rh⁻ mother an anti-Rh antibody injection (Rho-GAM) soon after the first delivery.

Figure Z4.2: Simplified blood clotting cascade — thromboplastin release activates the prothrombin–thrombin–fibrinogen–fibrin sequence, forming a clot mesh.

Blood clotting (coagulation) is a protective mechanism that plugs an injured blood vessel, preventing excessive blood loss. It involves a cascade of ~13 clotting factors (numbered I–XIII, most synthesised in the liver) activating each other in sequence, triggered through two converging pathways:

PathwayTriggerSpeed
Extrinsic pathwayTissue damage releases thromboplastin (tissue factor) from injured vessel wall / surrounding tissuesFast — main route in vivo
Intrinsic pathwayContact of blood with exposed collagen at the injury site activates factors already present in blood/plateletsSlower, several steps

Both pathways converge on activating Factor X, which converts prothrombin → thrombin (an enzyme) in the presence of Ca²⁺ (Factor IV). Thrombin then converts soluble fibrinogen → insoluble fibrin threads, which form a mesh that traps RBCs and platelets to form the clot. Vitamin K is essential for the liver's synthesis of several clotting factors (II, VII, IX, X), and heparin (released by basophils/mast cells and also present in blood) acts as a natural anticoagulant that prevents clotting inside intact vessels.

NEET point: Haemophilia is an X-linked recessive disorder in which clotting factor VIII (haemophilia A) or IX (haemophilia B) is deficient, causing delayed/excessive bleeding even from minor cuts. Also remember: platelets release factors that cause vasoconstriction and platelet plug formation even before the full clotting cascade completes.

3. Lymph (Tissue Fluid)

As blood passes through capillaries under hydrostatic pressure, some plasma (water, small solutes, but minus large proteins) filters out into the intercellular spaces of tissues, forming interstitial/tissue fluid. Most of this fluid diffuses back into capillaries, but the remainder is picked up by a separate network of blind-ended lymph capillaries and becomes lymph — a colourless, alkaline fluid similar to plasma but with much less protein, and rich in lymphocytes.

Lymphatic pathway: Lymph capillaries → larger lymph vessels (with valves, like veins, to prevent backflow) → lymph nodes (filter/cleanse lymph and add lymphocytes/antibodies) → lymph ducts — the thoracic duct (drains the lower body, left arm, and left side of head/neck/thorax into the left subclavian vein) and the right lymphatic duct (drains the right upper part of the body) — which finally empty lymph back into the blood via the subclavian veins.

FeatureBloodLymph
ColourRed (haemoglobin)Colourless / pale yellow
ProteinsHigh (albumin, globulin, fibrinogen)Low
RBCsPresentAbsent
WBCsPresent (all types)Mainly lymphocytes
Flow directionTwo-way (heart to tissues and back)One-way only, toward the heart
Functions of lymph: (i) returns tissue fluid and filtered plasma proteins back to the blood, maintaining blood volume and interstitial fluid balance; (ii) transports absorbed dietary fats from intestinal villi (via specialised lacteals) as chyle, bypassing the liver initially; (iii) lymph nodes filter out foreign particles/pathogens and are sites where lymphocytes are activated — central to the body's immune/defence mechanism.

4. Human Heart — Structure

The human heart is roughly fist-sized, located in the thoracic cavity (mediastinum, slightly tilted to the left), and enclosed in a double-layered protective sac called the pericardium, with pericardial fluid between the layers reducing friction. The heart wall has three layers: the outer epicardium, the thick middle myocardium (cardiac muscle — responsible for contraction) and the inner endocardium lining the chambers.

The heart is myogenic (initiates its own rhythmic beat, unlike skeletal muscle which needs a nerve impulse) and has four chambers — two upper thin-walled atria (receiving chambers) and two lower thick-walled ventricles (pumping chambers, with the left ventricle wall thickest since it pumps blood to the entire body), separated by the interatrial and interventricular septa which keep oxygenated and deoxygenated blood from mixing.

Figure Z4.3: Four-chambered human heart — right side (deoxygenated blood) separated from left side (oxygenated blood) by septa; tricuspid and bicuspid valves prevent backflow between atria and ventricles.

Besides the atrioventricular valves, the heart has two semilunar valves — the pulmonary valve (between right ventricle and pulmonary artery) and the aortic valve (between left ventricle and aorta) — that prevent backflow of blood into the ventricles once ejected. All four valves ensure blood flows in one direction only.

Chamber / ValveLocationRole
Right atriumReceives from superior & inferior vena cava, coronary sinusCollects deoxygenated blood from body
Tricuspid valveBetween right atrium & right ventricle3 cusps; prevents backflow into right atrium
Right ventriclePumps to lungs via pulmonary arteryPulmonary/semilunar valve prevents backflow
Left atriumReceives from pulmonary veins (4)Collects oxygenated blood from lungs
Bicuspid (Mitral) valveBetween left atrium & left ventricle2 cusps; prevents backflow into left atrium
Left ventriclePumps to body via aorta (thickest wall)Aortic/semilunar valve prevents backflow

The heart muscle itself is supplied with oxygenated blood by the coronary arteries (branching from the aorta just above the aortic valve) — blockage of these vessels by fatty/cholesterol deposits underlies coronary artery disease.

The heart has a specialised conduction system that initiates and coordinates each beat: the Sino-Atrial Node (SAN), a patch of nodal tissue in the wall of the right atrium (the "pacemaker" — it generates the highest rate of impulses, ~70–75/min, so sets the overall heart rate), which spreads excitation to the Atrio-Ventricular Node (AVN) located in the lower-right corner of the interatrial septum. From the AVN, the impulse travels via the AV bundle (Bundle of His) — the only muscular connection between atria and ventricles — which divides into left and right bundle branches within the interventricular septum, terminating in fine Purkinje fibres that rapidly spread the impulse through the ventricular walls, causing near-simultaneous ventricular contraction.

5. Cardiac Cycle and ECG

One complete heartbeat — comprising a sequence of contraction (systole) and relaxation (diastole) of the atria and ventricles — is a cardiac cycle, lasting about 0.8 seconds at a resting heart rate of ~72–75 beats/minute.

PhaseDurationWhat Happens
Joint diastole~0.4 sAtria & ventricles both relaxed; blood flows passively from veins into atria and on into ventricles through open AV valves (~70% of ventricular filling happens here, before atrial systole even begins)
Atrial systole~0.1 sSAN impulse contracts both atria together, pushing the remaining ~30% of blood into the ventricles (AV valves open, semilunar valves closed)
Ventricular systole~0.3 sVentricles contract; pressure rise closes AV valves ("lub"), then opens semilunar valves to eject blood into pulmonary artery & aorta

Each cycle produces two audible heart sounds via a stethoscope: "lub" (first sound — closure of tricuspid & bicuspid/AV valves at the start of ventricular systole) and "dub" (second sound — closure of the semilunar valves at the start of ventricular diastole, as backflowing blood snaps them shut).

Figure Z4.4: A normal ECG trace showing the P wave, QRS complex, and T wave that correspond to the electrical events of one cardiac cycle.
ECG WaveRepresents
P waveDepolarisation (excitation) of both atria, immediately followed by atrial systole
QRS complexDepolarisation of the ventricles, marking the start of ventricular systole; largest deflection since ventricular muscle mass is greatest
T waveRepolarisation (recovery) of the ventricles, marking the end of ventricular systole

The stroke volume (SV) — the volume of blood pumped by one ventricle in one beat — is about 70 mL. Cardiac output (CO) = Stroke volume × Heart rate; with SV ≈ 70 mL and heart rate ≈ 72/min, CO ≈ 5000 mL (5 L) per minute — meaning the heart pumps roughly the body's entire blood volume every minute. Cardiac output rises during exercise mainly via an increased heart rate and stronger contraction (increased SV).

NEET point: Total cardiac cycle time = 0.8 s → theoretical max heart rate ≈ 75/min at rest. Remember the sequence: SAN → spreads over atria → AVN (slight delay here allows atria to finish contracting before ventricles start) → AV bundle → bundle branches → Purkinje fibres → ventricular contraction. A damaged SAN can be substituted clinically by an artificial pacemaker.

6. Double Circulation and Regulation

Human blood passes through the heart twice in one complete circuit — double circulation — an arrangement that keeps oxygenated and deoxygenated blood completely separate, allowing efficient, high-pressure delivery of oxygen to tissues. It is made up of two circuits:

Figure Z4.5: Double circulation — the pulmonary circuit (heart ↔ lungs, for oxygenation) and the systemic circuit (heart ↔ body tissues, for delivering oxygenated blood), both passing through the heart.
CircuitPathBlood Carried
Pulmonary circulationRight ventricle → pulmonary artery → lungs → pulmonary veins → left atriumPulmonary artery: deoxygenated (unusual — the only artery carrying deoxygenated blood); pulmonary vein: oxygenated
Systemic circulationLeft ventricle → aorta → body tissues → venae cavae → right atriumAorta: oxygenated; venae cavae: deoxygenated

Cardiac activity is myogenic (the SAN initiates the beat on its own, without needing a nerve signal to start), but its rate is finely modulated by a cardiac centre in the medulla oblongata of the brain. This centre can send signals via the sympathetic nervous system (releases noradrenaline, increases heart rate & force of contraction) or via the parasympathetic (vagus) nerve (releases acetylcholine, decreases heart rate) — reaching the heart's pacemaker and neutralising each other's effects to fine-tune rate to the body's needs (e.g. increasing during exercise/stress, decreasing at rest). Hormones from the adrenal medulla (adrenaline & noradrenaline) can also directly increase heart rate and cardiac output, especially under stress ("fight or flight").

Blood pressure (BP) is the pressure exerted by circulating blood on vessel walls, normally expressed as systolic/diastolic — a healthy young adult's resting BP is about 120/80 mmHg (120 = systolic, the pressure during ventricular systole; 80 = diastolic, the pressure during ventricular diastole), measured using a sphygmomanometer.

DisorderDescription
HypertensionPersistently elevated BP (≥140/90 mmHg); increases risk of heart disease and affects vital organs like kidneys, brain, heart
Coronary Artery Disease (Atherosclerosis)Deposition of fat, cholesterol and fibrous tissue on the inner walls of coronary arteries, narrowing their lumen (occlusion) and reducing blood flow to heart muscle
Angina (angina pectoris)Chest pain due to insufficient oxygen supply to heart muscle, often triggered by exertion/stress, without permanent muscle damage
Myocardial Infarction (Heart Attack)Sudden, severe reduction/blockage of blood supply (usually a coronary artery) causes death of a portion of heart muscle
Heart failureHeart's pumping efficiency drops so much it can't meet the body's needs; often called congestive heart failure as blood backs up in veins leading to congestion of lungs/other organs — not the same as cardiac arrest (complete stopping of the heart)
NEET point: Normal resting BP = 120/80 mmHg; a rise of ≥20 mmHg systolic or ≥10 mmHg diastolic above this is considered hypertension. Remember heart failure ≠ heart attack ≠ cardiac arrest — these are three distinct, commonly confused terms in NEET MCQs. Also note the pulmonary artery and pulmonary vein are exceptions to the usual artery-carries-oxygenated / vein-carries-deoxygenated rule.
Chapter 5 topics

Ch 5 Excretory Products and their Elimination

Metabolic activity constantly generates waste — chiefly nitrogenous compounds from the breakdown (catabolism) of proteins and nucleic acids — which must be removed from the body or they become toxic. The process of removing these harmful metabolic wastes is called excretion. Animals excrete ammonia, urea, uric acid, CO₂ and water in different proportions depending on habitat and water availability. In humans, this job is carried out chiefly by a pair of kidneys, assisted by the lungs, liver and skin. This chapter covers the modes of nitrogenous excretion, the anatomy of the human excretory system, the structure of the nephron, the physiology of urine formation (filtration, reabsorption, secretion), the countercurrent mechanism that concentrates urine, hormonal regulation of kidney function, micturition, and common disorders — all extremely high-yield for NEET.

1. Modes of Nitrogenous Excretion

Deamination of amino acids releases toxic ammonia (NH₃) as the primary nitrogenous waste. Depending on how much water is available and how toxic a waste an animal can tolerate, this ammonia is either voided directly or converted into less toxic compounds (urea or uric acid) before excretion — this is a major NEET-favourite classification.

CategoryWaste ExcretedToxicity / Water NeedExamples
AmmonotelismAmmonia (directly, no conversion)Highly toxic — needs large amounts of water to be washed out/diluted rapidly; readily soluble & diffuses out easilyMost bony (teleost) fishes, aquatic amphibians, aquatic insects, Protozoa (e.g. Amoeba, via general body surface/diffusion)
UreotelismUrea (ammonia converted to urea in the liver via the ornithine cycle, then excreted, mostly by kidneys)Less toxic than ammonia; needs comparatively less water; some urea can be retained/reabsorbed in kidney tubules to help concentrate urineMammals (incl. humans), many terrestrial amphibians, marine fishes, sea/marine turtles
UricotelismUric acid (semi-solid, insoluble, pellet/paste form)Least toxic; can be excreted with minimal water loss — key adaptation for conserving water in dry/aerial habitats or inside a shelled eggReptiles, birds, land snails, insects
Figure Z5.1: The three modes of nitrogenous excretion, arranged by increasing water conservation and decreasing toxicity of the excreted product.

Some invertebrates and larval forms show a transition between modes as habitat changes — e.g. the tadpole larva of a frog (aquatic) is ammonotelic, but on metamorphosis into an adult frog (semi-terrestrial), it switches to ureotelism. This shift, called uricotelism/ureotelism transition, is directly tied to a change in water availability and is a classic NEET assertion-reason question.

NEET point: Uric acid is synthesised mainly to conserve water, not because it is chemically "better" — it is nearly insoluble in water and is excreted as a semi-solid paste/pellet, ideal for animals laying shelled (cleidoic) eggs, where liquid nitrogenous waste cannot be voided during development. Humans are ureotelic but also excrete small amounts of uric acid (from purine breakdown) and ammonia.

2. Human Excretory System — Organs

The human excretory system consists of a pair of kidneys, a pair of ureters, a single urinary bladder and a single urethra.

Figure Z5.2: Human urinary system — paired kidneys receive blood from the renal (abdominal) aorta, filtrate collects and drains via ureters into the urinary bladder and is voided via the urethra.

Kidneys are reddish-brown, bean-shaped structures situated between the level of the last thoracic and third lumbar vertebra, one on each side of the vertebral column, close to the dorsal inner wall of the abdominal cavity (retroperitoneal). Each kidney of an adult human is about 10–12 cm long, 5–7 cm wide, 2–3 cm thick, with an average weight of 120–170 g. Towards the centre of the inner concave surface is a notch called the hilum, through which the renal artery, renal vein and ureter enter/leave; just inside the hilum lies a funnel-shaped space, the renal pelvis, with projections called calyces.

Internally, the kidney has two zones — an outer renal cortex and an inner renal medulla. The medulla is divided into 8–12 conical masses called medullary/renal pyramids projecting into the calyces (their apices, called papillae, open into the minor calyces). The cortex extends in between the medullary pyramids as renal columns of Bertini.

OrganDescription / Function
Renal arteryBrings oxygenated, nutrient- and waste-laden blood into the kidney (from the abdominal aorta)
Renal veinCarries filtered (purified) blood away from the kidney to the inferior vena cava
Ureter (2)Muscular tube carrying urine from renal pelvis of each kidney to the urinary bladder by peristalsis
Urinary bladderSmooth, muscular, distensible sac that stores urine temporarily before micturition
UrethraTube through which urine is finally discharged from the bladder to outside via the urinary meatus
NEET point: The functional unit of the kidney is the nephron, not the pyramid — each kidney contains about 1–1.3 million nephrons. Also note: the kidney's outer surface is enclosed by a tough protective capsule called the fibrous/renal capsule, and the position of kidneys is retroperitoneal (behind the peritoneum), a frequently tested anatomical detail.

3. Nephron — Structural and Functional Unit

Each nephron has two main parts: a cup-shaped Malpighian/renal corpuscle and a long, coiled renal tubule. The renal tubule begins with a double-walled cup, the Bowman's capsule, which encloses a cluster of capillaries — the glomerulus — formed from an afferent arteriole (wider) that branches into capillaries and then reunites into an efferent arteriole (narrower) leaving the capsule. This difference in the diameter of afferent and efferent arterioles is what generates the hydrostatic pressure needed for filtration.

Figure Z5.3: Schematic nephron — Malpighian corpuscle (glomerulus + Bowman's capsule) → PCT → Loop of Henle (descending + ascending limbs) → DCT → collecting duct.

The renal tubule of a nephron has four regions:

RegionLocation / StructureMain Role
Proximal Convoluted Tubule (PCT)Lies close to the Bowman's capsule, in the cortex; lined by simple cuboidal brush-border (microvilli) epithelium — increases surface area for reabsorptionReabsorbs ~70–80% of filtrate (glucose, amino acids, Na⁺, water, most electrolytes); maintains filtrate pH & osmolarity
Loop of Henle (Henle's loop)Hairpin-shaped; descending limb (thin, permeable to water, impermeable to salts) dips from cortex into medulla, ascending limb (thick, impermeable to water, actively/passively transports NaCl) returns to cortexEstablishes/maintains the medullary osmotic (concentration) gradient — key to concentrating urine
Distal Convoluted Tubule (DCT)In the cortex; lined by cuboidal epithelium, no brush border; receives filtrate from ascending limbConditional/selective reabsorption of Na⁺ and water (hormone-regulated); reabsorbs HCO₃⁻; secretes H⁺, K⁺, NH₃ — maintains ionic & acid-base balance
Collecting DuctExtends from cortex through medulla to renal pelvis; receives filtrate from many nephrons; the DCTs of several nephrons open into itReabsorbs large amounts of water (ADH-dependent — makes final urine concentrated or dilute); passes urine to renal pelvis → ureter

Nephrons are of two types based on the location of the corpuscle and length of the loop of Henle:

  • Cortical nephrons (~85%): Corpuscle in the outer cortex, with a short loop of Henle that dips only slightly into the medulla.
  • Juxtamedullary nephrons (~15%): Corpuscle lies close to the cortex-medulla junction, with a very long loop of Henle that penetrates deep into the medulla — these are chiefly responsible for producing concentrated urine.

A unique blood supply, the vasa recta — a network of thin-walled capillaries that runs parallel to the Henle's loop — is associated with juxtamedullary nephrons and plays a vital role in maintaining the medullary gradient (it is absent or highly reduced around cortical nephrons).

NEET point: The filtration membrane through which the glomerular filtrate passes has three layers (inside to outside as blood flows): (1) endothelium of glomerular blood capillaries (thin & fenestrated), (2) glomerular basement membrane (GBM), and (3) epithelium of Bowman's capsule (podocytes, with filtration slits/pedicels). Together this membrane acts as a molecular sieve preventing blood cells and large proteins from entering the filtrate.

4. Urine Formation — Filtration, Reabsorption & Secretion

Urine formation involves three sequential processes occurring in different parts of the nephron: glomerular filtration, tubular reabsorption, and tubular secretion.

(a) Glomerular Filtration. Blood is filtered through the glomerular capillary walls into the Bowman's capsule — this ultrafiltration process is called glomerular filtration, and the fluid produced is the glomerular filtrate. This is a bulk-flow process driven by hydrostatic (blood) pressure, opposed by glomerular capillary blood colloid osmotic pressure and capsular hydrostatic pressure — the net pressure is called the net filtration pressure (NFP).

TermMeaning
Renal blood flow (RBF)Kidneys receive ~1,100–1,200 mL/min blood (~20–25% of cardiac output) — a very rich blood supply for their size
Glomerular Filtration Rate (GFR)Volume of filtrate formed by both kidneys per minute; in a healthy adult, ~125 mL/min ≈ 180 L/day — yet only about 1–1.5 L urine is produced daily due to massive reabsorption (~99%)
Juxtaglomerular Apparatus (JGA)Specialised sensory cells at the point where the distal tubule lies in contact with the afferent (and efferent) arteriole; monitors changes in blood flow/filtrate flow and helps regulate GFR (via renin release)

A fall in GFR activates the JGA to release renin, which triggers the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS), which in turn raises glomerular blood pressure and restores GFR — a negative-feedback autoregulatory mechanism (detailed in section 6).

(b) Reabsorption. Filtrate passing down the tubule is not urine — most of it is reabsorbed by the tubular epithelial cells, actively or passively, back into blood via the peritubular capillaries surrounding the tubule. Substances like glucose, amino acids, Na⁺ and most water are reabsorbed by active transport (requiring energy), while some ions and water move by passive transport (diffusion/osmosis, following the electrochemical/osmotic gradient set up by active transport).

RegionWhat's ReabsorbedMode
PCT~70–80% of filtrate — glucose, amino acids, Na⁺, K⁺, most water, HCO₃⁻, ~all nutrientsAlmost entirely active (some passive)
Descending limb of Henle's loopWater only (permeable to water, not salts) — filtrate becomes progressively more concentrated as it descendsPassive (osmosis)
Ascending limb of Henle's loopElectrolytes/NaCl (impermeable to water) — filtrate becomes dilute as it ascendsThick segment: active transport of NaCl; thin segment: passive diffusion
DCTConditional reabsorption of Na⁺ and water (regulated by aldosterone); HCO₃⁻ reabsorbedActive (hormone-dependent)
Collecting ductLarge amounts of water (ADH-dependent, especially during water scarcity); some NaCl and ureaPassive (ADH-mediated water permeability)

(c) Secretion. The tubule also actively adds certain substances from peritubular capillary blood into the filtrate — this is tubular secretion, the reverse of reabsorption. It occurs mainly in the DCT and helps maintain ionic and acid-base (pH) balance of body fluids.

Substances SecretedRegionPurpose
H⁺, K⁺, NH₃ (ammonia), creatinine, drug metabolitesChiefly DCT (some in PCT)Maintains blood pH and Na⁺-K⁺ balance; eliminates foreign substances/excess ions

The tubular fluid, now called urine, passes from DCT → collecting duct → renal pelvis → ureter → urinary bladder. On average, a healthy human excretes about 1–1.5 L of urine per day. Normal urine is about 95% water and 5% nitrogenous wastes (urea, uric acid, creatinine) and other solutes; its pH is around 6 (slightly acidic), and its specific gravity is roughly 1.008–1.030.

NEET point: Sequence to remember — Filtration (glomerulus, bulk flow, non-selective except for size/charge) → Reabsorption (mostly PCT, selective, active + passive) → Secretion (mostly DCT, active). Only about 1% of the ~180 L/day filtrate leaves the body as urine (~1–1.5 L/day) — the rest (~99%) is reabsorbed, underscoring how central reabsorption is to renal physiology.

5. Concentration of the Filtrate — Countercurrent Mechanism

Humans can produce urine much more concentrated than blood plasma — an essential adaptation for conserving water. This is achieved by the countercurrent mechanism, made possible because the Henle's loop and the vasa recta run parallel to each other but with fluid flowing in opposite directions (counter-current) within their limbs, operating mainly in juxtamedullary nephrons.

Figure Z5.4: Countercurrent mechanism — an increasing osmolarity gradient from cortex (~300 mOsm/L) to inner medulla (~1200 mOsm/L) is set up by the loop of Henle and maintained by the vasa recta.

How the gradient is built and used:

  • As filtrate flows down the descending limb (permeable to water, not to solutes), water diffuses out into the increasingly salty medullary interstitium, and the filtrate becomes progressively more concentrated as it moves toward the tip of the loop.
  • As filtrate flows up the ascending limb (impermeable to water, but actively transports NaCl out), electrolytes are pumped out into the medullary interstitium, and the filtrate becomes progressively dilute as it moves back toward the cortex — this active NaCl transport is precisely what creates the high osmolarity of the medulla in the first place.
  • The vasa recta, running parallel and also in countercurrent fashion, removes water gained from the interstitium without washing away the salt gradient, thereby helping maintain (not create) the gradient.
  • As the collecting duct passes back down through this hyperosmotic medullary gradient, water diffuses out of it (if ADH makes the duct permeable), concentrating the urine further before it is released.

This entire arrangement — descending limb, ascending limb and vasa recta running counter to each other and to the collecting duct — is termed the countercurrent multiplier system, and it is this mechanism that allows humans to produce urine as concentrated as roughly 4x plasma osmolarity when needed (e.g. during dehydration).

NEET point: Do not confuse the two limbs' permeability — descending limb: permeable to water, impermeable to electrolytes; ascending limb: impermeable to water, permeable/actively transports electrolytes. This exact pairing is one of the most frequently asked single-line facts in this chapter.

6. Regulation of Kidney Function & Micturition

Kidney function is under precise hormonal and neural control so that GFR, and hence body fluid volume, ionic balance and blood pressure, stays within a narrow normal range.

RegulatorSource / TriggerMain Effect
Antidiuretic Hormone / Vasopressin (ADH)Released from the neurohypophysis (posterior pituitary); secretion increases when body is dehydrated / blood volume & BP fall / plasma osmolarity rises (detected by osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus)Increases permeability of DCT & collecting duct to water → more water reabsorbed → concentrated urine, low volume ("antidiuresis"); also has a vasoconstrictor effect that raises BP
Renin–Angiotensin–Aldosterone System (RAAS)Fall in glomerular blood flow/GFR/BP or blood volume is sensed by the JGA, which releases reninRenin converts angiotensinogen (plasma protein, from liver) → angiotensin I → (via ACE, mainly in lungs) angiotensin II, a powerful vasoconstrictor that directly raises glomerular BP (restoring GFR) and stimulates the adrenal cortex to release aldosterone, which causes reabsorption of Na⁺ and water at DCT (raising blood volume/BP) — an important negative-feedback loop
Atrial Natriuretic Factor (ANF)Released by the walls of the atria of the heart when blood volume/blood pressure increases (atrial stretch)Acts as a vasodilator and antagonist of RAAS — decreases blood pressure by causing natriuresis (increased Na⁺ and water excretion), lowering BP
