Chapter 3: The Living World

The Earth contains millions of organisms differing in size, shape, habitat, nutrition and reproduction. This variety is called Biodiversity — a term popularised by W.G. Rosen (1985) referring to the diversity of organisms at all levels, from genes to ecosystems, that exists on Earth. Estimates place the total number of species (described plus undescribed) anywhere from 1.7 million (described so far) to over 8–30 million if unstudied groups such as insects, fungi and marine organisms are included.

What defines "living"? NCERT is explicit that there is no single defining feature of life that applies to every living organism without exception — even growth, reproduction and consciousness have exceptions (see below). The most technically accurate way to define life is: metabolism is the only defining property common to all living organisms, without exception, though it too can be replicated cell-free in a test tube, so ultimately the term "life" is best understood as a functional definition covering self-replication, self-organisation, response to stimuli and metabolic activity taken together, and it is the individual (organism) that truly "lives", not its isolated chemical components.

Characteristics of Living Organisms

1. Growth

  • Increase in size and mass — of cells, tissues or the whole organism.
  • Plants show unlimited/indeterminate growth throughout their life (open growth, via meristems).
  • Animals show limited/determinate growth — grow up to a certain age, then stop.
  • Intrinsic vs extrinsic growth: living organisms grow from the inside (intrinsic — by an increase in cell number/cell division and cell mass), whereas non-living things like crystals or mountains grow by external accumulation of material on their surface (extrinsic/accretion).
  • Growth alone is not a defining property — non-living crystals also "grow," and unicellular organisms increasing in cell number is reproduction, not growth in the multicellular sense; also, growth in plants can be measured but the exact same growth pattern doesn't apply uniformly to all organisms.

2. Reproduction

  • Asexual reproduction: A single parent produces offspring without gamete fusion — e.g. binary fission in Amoeba, budding in Hydra/yeast, fragmentation, or vegetative propagation in plants.
  • Sexual reproduction: Two parents contribute gametes that fuse to form a zygote — e.g. Human, Mango.
  • Exceptions (why reproduction isn't a universal defining feature): many organisms — mules, sterile worker bees/ants, and most infertile individuals — do not reproduce at all, yet are undeniably alive. Similarly, many unicellular organisms don't clearly separate "growth" from "reproduction," since increase in cell number IS both.

3. Metabolism

  • Sum of all the chemical reactions occurring inside the body of a living organism, made possible by a highly ordered, specific set of enzyme-catalysed steps.
  • Anabolism: Constructive/building-up reactions (synthesis of complex molecules from simpler ones) — e.g. photosynthesis, protein synthesis.
  • Catabolism: Destructive/breaking-down reactions (complex molecules broken into simpler ones, usually releasing energy) — e.g. respiration, digestion.
  • Defining property of life without exception — every living organism, from a single bacterial cell to a giant tree, shows metabolism, and no non-living object does. However, isolated metabolic reactions (an enzyme catalysing its substrate) can also be demonstrated in vitro in a cell-free system, which is "metabolism" in a chemical sense but is NOT called "living" — this is a classic NCERT/NEET trick point: metabolism is necessary but the reactions themselves, outside a cell, are not living.

4. Cellular Organisation

All living organisms are made of one or more cells — the cell is the basic structural and functional unit of life (Cell Theory).

Unicellular organisms (e.g. bacteria, Amoeba, Paramecium, Chlamydomonas) are single cells that independently carry out all life functions — nutrition, respiration, excretion, reproduction — within that one cell. Multicellular organisms show division of labour — cells are organised into tissues, tissues into organs, and organs into organ systems, each specialised for a particular function, making the whole organism far more efficient and complex than a simple collection of identical cells.

5. Consciousness

Ability to sense and respond to environmental stimuli (light, temperature, water, chemicals, gravity, sound, touch, etc.) — considered by NCERT to be the most defining and universal characteristic of living organisms, shown by every organism from a bacterium to a human.

Plants also show consciousness even though they lack a nervous system — e.g. a potted plant kept in the dark and then exposed to light bends towards the light source (phototropism); the response is mediated by hormones rather than neurons. Humans are considered the only organism truly "aware" of themselves (self-consciousness), but the ability to sense and react to stimuli is shown throughout the living world.

Taxonomy

Taxonomy is the branch of biology dealing with the study, characterisation, identification, nomenclature and classification of organisms. Coined by A.P. de Candolle, it involves several distinct processes:

  • Identification: Determining the correct name and taxonomic position of an organism by comparing its characters with already known/described organisms.
  • Nomenclature: Assigning a scientific (universally accepted) name to an organism, based on agreed international rules — governed by the ICBN (International Code of Botanical Nomenclature, now ICN) for plants and ICZN (International Code of Zoological Nomenclature) for animals.
  • Classification: The process of arranging organisms into convenient categories/groups based on similarities, differences and evolutionary relationships, making their identification, comprehension and study easier.
  • Systematics — the broader field studying the diversity of organisms and their evolutionary relationships; it encompasses identification, nomenclature and classification. The term comes from the Latin "systema" meaning systematic arrangement, and it also incorporates knowledge from morphology, anatomy, physiology, biochemistry, and evolutionary studies to establish relationships among organisms.
Father of Taxonomy: Carolus Linnaeus
Figure 3.1: Taxonomy in practice — Systematics is the umbrella field built on the other three

Taxonomic Hierarchy

Species → Genus → Family → Order → Class → Phylum/Division → Kingdom

This ranked series of categories is called a taxonomic hierarchy, established by Linnaeus. Each category/rank is called a taxon (plural: taxa) and represents a unit of classification — e.g. "Insecta" is a taxon at the rank of Class. As you move up the hierarchy from Species to Kingdom, the number of common characteristics between organisms in that taxon decreases and the number of organisms/specificity increases — Species is the smallest, most fundamental and most specific unit (a group of individuals with fundamental similarities that can interbreed and produce fertile offspring), while Kingdom is the broadest, most inclusive category.

Intermediate/additional categories are sometimes inserted for finer classification — e.g. sub-species, sub-family, super-family, sub-order, sub-class, sub-phylum/sub-division — particularly useful for groups with very large numbers of species.

Figure 3.2: Taxonomic hierarchy — broadest category (Kingdom) at the top, narrowing to the most specific (Species)
CategoryHuman (Homo sapiens)Mango (Mangifera indica)
KingdomAnimaliaPlantae
Phylum / DivisionChordataAngiospermae
ClassMammaliaDicotyledonae
OrderPrimataSapindales
FamilyHominidaeAnacardiaceae
GenusHomoMangifera
Speciessapiensindica
NEET point: "Phylum" is used for animals, while "Division" is the equivalent rank used for plants — a frequently tested terminology distinction.

Taxonomical Aids

  • Herbarium
  • Botanical Garden
  • Museum
  • Zoological Park
  • Key
  • Flora
  • Manual
  • Monograph
Figure 3.3: Taxonomical aids grouped by type
AidDescription
HerbariumA store-house of collected plant specimens that are dried, pressed, preserved on sheets, and arranged systematically according to a widely accepted classification system; each sheet also carries a label with date/place of collection, English/local/vernacular names, and the collector's name.
Botanical GardenGardens where living plants are grown and maintained for reference; each plant is labelled indicating its scientific name and family. Famous examples: Royal Botanical Gardens, Kew (England); Indian Botanical Garden, Howrah, Kolkata; National Botanical Research Institute, Lucknow.
MuseumPreserve plant and animal specimens for study and reference — specimens may be preserved in preservative solutions (like formalin) or as dry specimens, and larger animal specimens are often kept as stuffed skins.
Zoological ParkPlaces where live wild animals are kept in protected/artificial environments for public viewing and to allow them to be studied for their food habits and behaviour.
KeyA taxonomic aid used for identification of organisms based on similarities and dissimilarities. Consists of a series of contrasting statements (called couplets) offering two alternative choices, each leading either to another couplet or to the identification/name of the taxon. Keys are usually analytical, and separate keys are needed for each taxonomic category. Keys are generally comparable to a dichotomous branching diagram.
FloraContains the actual account of habitat and distribution of plants of a given area — provides information/data for identification of names of plants found in that particular area.
ManualUseful in providing information for identification of names of plants/animals of any given area.
MonographContains information on any one taxon (a single genus or family, for example), providing comprehensive and complete details for that group.
CatalogueProvides an inventory list of species found in a particular area, along with brief, precise information about their identification.

Scientific Names

Binomial nomenclature, the two-word naming system, was given by Carolus Linnaeus and is now universally accepted by biologists across the world for naming living organisms. Universal rules ensure that each organism has a name that is unique and remains the same everywhere, avoiding confusion caused by local/vernacular names.

Figure 3.4: Binomial nomenclature structure

Rules of nomenclature (ICBN/ICZN — commonly tested):

  • Biological names are generally in Latin and written in italics, since Latin is a "dead" language and its usage/meaning does not change over time.
  • The first word (Genus) always begins with a capital letter; the second word (specific epithet) begins with a small/lowercase letter.
  • When handwritten, both words of the name must be separately underlined (since italics cannot be shown by hand) to indicate their Latin origin.
  • The name of the author is often written in an abbreviated form after the species name at the time of first description — e.g. Mangifera indica Linn. indicates that this species was first described by Linnaeus.
OrganismScientific Name
HumanHomo sapiens
MangoMangifera indica
WheatTriticum aestivum
LionPanthera leo
TigerPanthera tigris

Chapter 4: Morphology of Flowering Plants

Angiosperms show incredible diversity in external form (morphology), yet every flowering plant shares the same basic body plan — a root system, a shoot system bearing stem and leaves, and (in the reproductive phase) inflorescences, flowers, fruits and seeds.

The Root

The primary root develops from the radicle and grows down into the soil. It fixes the plant and absorbs water and minerals.

Fig: Tap root, fibrous root and adventitious (prop) root systems

Tap Root System

  • Direct elongation of the radicle forms the primary root, which bears secondary and tertiary roots.
  • The primary root and its branches together form the tap root system.
  • e.g. Mustard, Mango, Pea (dicots).

Fibrous Root System

  • The primary root is short-lived and is replaced by a large number of roots.
  • These originate from the base of the stem and form the fibrous root system.
  • e.g. Wheat, Rice, Maize (monocots).

Adventitious Roots

  • Roots that arise from parts of the plant other than the radicle.
  • e.g. Banyan (hanging prop roots), Grass, Monstera.

Functions & Regions of the Root

Functions

  • Absorption of water and minerals.
  • Providing anchorage to the plant.
  • Storing reserve food material.
  • Synthesis of plant growth regulators.

Regions (apex → base)

  • Root cap — thimble-like structure at the apex; protects the tip.
  • Region of meristematic activity — small, thin-walled, densely-packed cells that divide repeatedly.
  • Region of elongation — cells enlarge rapidly, responsible for growth in length.
  • Region of maturation — cells differentiate; epidermal cells form root hairs that absorb water and minerals.
Fig: Regions of the root — maturation (root hairs), elongation, meristematic activity, root cap

Root Modifications

TypeModificationExample(s)
StorageTap root swells to store foodCarrot, Turnip
Adventitious root swells to store foodSweet potato
SupportProp roots — hang from branches to the ground for supportBanyan tree
Stilt roots — arise from lower stem nodes for extra supportSugarcane, Maize
BreathingRoots grow vertically upward for gas exchange (pneumatophores)Rhizophora (mangroves)

The Stem

  • Develops from the plumule; bears branches, leaves, flowers and fruits.
  • Bears nodes (where leaves arise) and internodes (region between two nodes).
  • Bears terminal and axillary buds.
  • Conducts water, minerals and photosynthates (transport function).
  • Performs storage, support, protection and vegetative propagation via its modifications.
CategoryModificationExample(s)
UndergroundStorage — TuberPotato
Storage — CormColocasia
Storage — RhizomeGinger, Turmeric
Storage — BulbOnion, Zaminkand
Sub-aerialRunner / Stolon (propagation)Grass, Strawberry
Offset (short internodes, rosette of leaves + tuft of roots)Pistia, Eichhornia
AerialTendrils (support, climbing)Gourds, Grapevine
Thorns (protection)Citrus, Bougainvillea
Phylloclade / fleshy photosynthetic stemOpuntia, Euphorbia
Fig: Common stem modifications — tuber, rhizome, bulb (underground) and thorn (aerial)
In banana, pineapple and Chrysanthemum, lateral branches arise from the basal underground part of the main stem, grow horizontally, then curve upward to give leafy shoots (suckers).

The Leaf

The leaf is a lateral, flat structure borne on the stem, developing from the shoot apical meristem (SAM) in acropetal order. It grows at a node and bears a bud (which develops into a branch) in its axil. Leaves are the chief photosynthetic organs.

Parts of a Leaf

  • Leaf base — attaches leaf to stem; may bear two lateral stipules; expands into a sheath in monocots.
  • Petiole — holds the blade to light; long, flexible petioles let the blade flutter, cooling it and refreshing the air around it.
  • Lamina (leaf blade) — the green expanded part with veins & veinlets that provide rigidity and transport water/minerals.
  • In some legumes the leaf base becomes swollen — called the pulvinus.

Venation

  • Reticulate — veinlets form a network; typical of dicots (e.g. Peepal).
  • Parallel — veins run parallel to each other within the lamina; typical of monocots (e.g. grasses).

Leaf Types

  • Simple leaf — lamina entire, or if incised the incisions don't touch the midrib.
  • Compound leaf — incisions reach the midrib, breaking it into leaflets; the axillary bud is present only at the base of the petiole, not at the base of a leaflet.
Fig: Parts of a leaf — leaf base with stipules, petiole and lamina (with midrib & veins)
Fig: Reticulate venation (network of veinlets) vs Parallel venation (veins run parallel)

Compound Leaf Types

  • Pinnately compound — leaflets borne on a common axis, the rachis (midrib equivalent). e.g. Neem.
  • Palmately compound — leaflets attached at a common point at the tip of the petiole. e.g. Silk cotton.

Phyllotaxy (arrangement on stem)

  • Alternate — one leaf per node. e.g. China rose, Mustard, Sunflower.
  • Opposite — a pair of leaves at each node. e.g. Calotropis, Guava.
  • Whorled — more than two leaves at a node, forming a whorl. e.g. Alstonia.
Fig: Phyllotaxy — alternate (China rose), opposite (Calotropis) and whorled (Alstonia)

Modifications of Leaves

ModificationFunctionExample(s)
TendrilsClimbingPea
SpinesDefenseCactus
Fleshy scale leaves (bulb)Food storageOnion, Garlic
Insectivorous / pitcher leavesTrap insects to manage nitrogen deficiencyPitcher plant, Venus flytrap
Phyllode (flattened green petiole)Photosynthesis (leaf itself is small & short-lived)Australian acacia

Inflorescence

  • The shoot apical meristem changes into a floral meristem; internodes stop elongating and the axis becomes condensed.
  • The apex produces floral appendages laterally at successive nodes instead of leaves.
  • The arrangement of flowers on the floral axis is called the inflorescence.

Racemose

The main axis keeps growing; flowers are borne laterally in acropetal succession (oldest at the base, youngest near the tip).

Cymose

The main axis terminates in a flower, so growth is limited; flowers are borne in basipetal order (youngest at the base). e.g. Datura, Hibiscus.

Fig: Racemose vs cymose inflorescence — order in which flowers open

The Flower

  • The reproductive unit of an angiosperm, meant for sexual reproduction.
  • Four whorls are arranged on the swollen end of the pedicel, called the receptacle / thalamus.
  • Calyx (sepals) and Corolla (petals) are accessory organs; when calyx & corolla are not distinct, together they are called the perianth (e.g. Lily).
  • Androecium (stamens) and Gynoecium (carpels) are the reproductive organs.
  • A flower with both androecium & gynoecium is bisexual; one with only one of them is unisexual (staminate or pistillate).
Fig: The four whorls of a flower on the thalamus — calyx, corolla, androecium and gynoecium

Symmetry

  • Actinomorphic (radial) — divisible into two equal halves along any radial plane. e.g. Mustard, Datura, Chilli.
  • Zygomorphic (bilateral) — divisible into equal halves in only one plane. e.g. Pea, Bean, Gulmohar, Cassia.
  • Asymmetric — cannot be divided into equal halves in any plane. e.g. Canna.

Merosity & Bract

  • Trimerous (3 members/whorl), Tetramerous (4), Pentamerous (5).
  • Bract — a reduced leaf found at the base of the pedicel.

Position on Thalamus

  • Hypogynous — gynoecium highest, ovary superior. e.g. Mustard, China rose, Brinjal.
  • Perigynous — gynoecium central, other whorls on the rim; ovary half-inferior. e.g. Plum, Rose, Peach.
  • Epigynous — thalamus grows up and fuses with the ovary; ovary inferior. e.g. Guava, Cucumber, sunflower ray florets.
Fig: Actinomorphic (radial, divisible in any plane) vs Zygomorphic (bilateral, one plane) flowers

Calyx & Corolla

  • Calyx — outermost whorl, members called sepals; protects the flower in bud stage. Gamosepalous (fused) or Polysepalous (free).
  • Corolla — members called petals, often brightly coloured to attract pollinators. Gamopetalous (fused) or Polypetalous (free).

Aestivation

The arrangement of sepals/petals in a floral bud relative to the other members of the same whorl.

  • Valvate — margins just touch, no overlap. e.g. Calotropis.
  • Twisted — one margin overlaps the next, and so on. e.g. China rose, Cotton, Ladyfinger.
  • Imbricate — margins overlap but not in any particular direction. e.g. Cassia, Gulmohar.
  • Vexillary — the largest (standard) petal overlaps the two wing petals, which overlap the two smallest (keel) petals. e.g. Pea, Bean.
Fig: Aestivation patterns — valvate (Calotropis), twisted (China rose), imbricate (Gulmohar), vexillary (Pea)

Androecium (Stamens)

Consists of stamens, each with a stalk (filament) and an anther. The anther is bilobed and tetrasporangiate, with four pollen sacs producing pollen grains. A sterile stamen is called a staminode.

ConditionDescriptionExample
PolyandrousStamens remain freeRose, Lotus
EpipetalousStamens attached to the petalsBrinjal
EpiphyllousStamens attached to the perianthLily
MonoadelphousStamens united into one bundleChina rose
DiadelphousStamens united into two bundlesPea
PolyadelphousStamens united into more than two bundlesCitrus
TetradynamousTwo outer short + four inner long stamensMustard
DidynamousFour stamens in two pairs of unequal lengthSalvia

Gynoecium (Carpels)

  • The female reproductive part, made up of one or more carpels; each carpel has a stigma (receptive surface for pollen), style (connects stigma to ovary) and ovary (enlarged basal part).
  • The ovary bears one or more ovules attached to a cushion-like placenta within a chamber called the locule.
  • Apocarpous — more than one free carpel (e.g. Lotus, Rose). Syncarpous — carpels fused together (e.g. Mustard, Tomato).
PlacentationDescriptionExample
MarginalPlacenta forms a ridge along the ventral suture; ovules in two rowsPea
AxilePlacenta axial, ovules attached to it in a multilocular ovaryChina rose, Tomato, Lemon
ParietalOvules on the inner wall; one-chambered ovary becomes two-chambered by a false septumMustard, Argemone
Free centralOvules borne on a central axis; septa absentDianthus, Primrose
BasalPlacenta at the base of the ovary; single ovule attachedSunflower, Marigold
Fig: Structure of a stamen and a carpel; example of axile placentation (ovules on a central axis)

The Fruit

  • A characteristic feature of flowering plants — a mature/ripened ovary developed after fertilisation.
  • A fruit formed without fertilisation of the ovary is called a parthenocarpic fruit (e.g. banana, pineapple, grapes — seedless varieties).
  • Consists of a wall (pericarp) and seeds. When thick and fleshy, the pericarp differentiates into outer epicarp, middle mesocarp and inner endocarp.
  • Mango and coconut are drupes — one-seeded fruits from monocarpellary superior ovaries. In mango the endocarp is stony hard; in coconut the mesocarp is fibrous.
Fig: Drupe (e.g. Mango) — pericarp differentiated into epicarp, mesocarp and endocarp, enclosing the seed

The Seed

Ovules develop into seeds after fertilisation. A seed has a seed coat and an embryo, and the embryo has a radicle, an embryonal axis and one (monocots) or two (dicots) cotyledons.

Dicot Seed

  • Seed coat has two layers — outer testa, inner tegmen.
  • Hilum — scar where the seed was attached to the fruit; above it lies the micropyle (small pore).
  • Embryo has an embryonal axis and two fleshy cotyledons full of reserve food.
  • Radicle and plumule lie at the two ends of the embryonal axis.
  • In Castor, endosperm (from double fertilisation) stores food — endospermous; in bean, gram, pea it is absent at maturity — non-endospermous.

Monocot Seed

  • One large, shield-shaped cotyledon — the scutellum — with a short axis bearing plumule and radicle.
  • Plumule and radicle are enclosed in sheaths — coleoptile and coleorhiza respectively.
  • Usually endospermic (bulky endosperm stores food); orchids are non-endospermic.
  • Endosperm's outer layer is a proteinous aleurone layer; seed coat is membranous, fused with the fruit wall.
  • Embryo is small, situated in a groove at one end of the endosperm.
Fig: Internal structure of a dicot seed (e.g. Bean) vs a monocot seed (e.g. Maize)

Floral Family Descriptions

1. Fabaceae (Papilionoideae)

Vegetative: root nodules; leaves alternate, pulvinate leaf base, stipulate.

Floral: Racemose; bisexual, zygomorphic; K(5) gamosepalous; C polypetalous, vexillary; A(9)+1 diadelphous; ovary superior, monocarpellary; fruit — legume; non-endospermic.

Br ⚥ K(5) C1+2+(2) A(9)+1 G1

Economic importance: Pulses (gram, arhar, moong, soyabean); edible oil (soyabean, groundnut); dye (Indigofera); fibre (Sunhemp); fodder (Sesbania, Trifolium); ornamental (Lupin, sweet pea); medicine (Muliathi).

2. Solanaceae

Vegetative: herbaceous, solid/hollow hairy stem; leaves alternate, exstipulate, simple.

Floral: Solitary, axillary or cymose; bisexual, actinomorphic; K(5) persistent; C(5) gamopetalous, valvate; A5 epipetalous; bicarpellary, syncarpous, bilocular, swollen placenta, hypogynous; fruit — berry/capsule; endospermic seed.

⊕ ⚥ K(5) C(5) A5 G(2)

Economic importance: Food (tomato, brinjal, potato); spice (chilli); medicine (Belladonna, ashwagandha); fumigatory (tobacco); ornamental (Petunia).

3. Brassicaceae

Vegetative: herbaceous, solid, branched stem; leaves simple, alternate, hairy.

Floral: Racemose; ebracteate, bisexual, actinomorphic, tetramerous; K 2+2 polysepalous, imbricate; C4 polypetalous; A6 polyandrous, tetradynamous (2+4); bicarpellary, syncarpous, bilobed, parietal placentation; fruit — siliqua; non-endospermic.

Ebr. ⊕ ⚥ K2+2 C4 A2+4 G(2)

4. Malvaceae

Vegetative: axillary inflorescence, alternate leaves, bracteate.

Floral: Actinomorphic; epicalyx present (a whorl of bracteoles around the calyx); K(5) gamosepalous; C5 polypetalous, epipetalous; monoadelphous androecium (filaments fused into one bundle); axile placentation, hypogynous; fruit — capsule.

Br ⊕ ⚥ Epi(3-7) K(5) C5 A(∞) G(5)

Economic importance: Food (okra, durian); fibre (cotton, jute); beverage (kola nut); timber (Balsa); ornamental (Hibiscus); medicinal (marshmallow root).

5. Poaceae

Vegetative: fibrous/adventitious/stilt roots (maize); hollow stem, exstipulate; alternate leaves, parallel venation, sheathy leaf base.

Floral: Inflorescence spike/spikelet (male spikelet = tassel, female = cob/ear); bisexual (rice) or unisexual (maize); perianth reduced to 2 lodicules; polyandrous; trimerous; monocarpellary superior ovary, basal placentation.

% ⚥ P2 A3+3 G1

6. Asteraceae (Compositae)

Vegetative: alternate/opposite (Helianthus)/whorled (Eupatorium) leaves, petiolate, exstipulate.

Floral: Capitulum inflorescence made of two floret types.

Ray florets: bracteate, zygomorphic, unisexual, ligulate corolla, androecium absent, gynoecium inferior with basal placentation.

Disc florets: bracteate, actinomorphic, bisexual, tubular corolla, 5 epipetalous syngenesious stamens, bicarpellary syncarpous inferior ovary, basal placentation.

Chapter 5: Biological Classification

Early classifications grouped all living organisms into just two kingdoms — Plantae and Animalia — based mainly on whether the organism was mobile, whether it could photosynthesise, and whether it had a cell wall. This two-kingdom system, credited to Linnaeus, was simple but had a fundamental flaw: it did not distinguish between the prokaryotes and eukaryotes, between unicellular and multicellular organisms, or between photosynthetic (autotrophic) and non-photosynthetic (heterotrophic) organisms. Many organisms — bacteria, fungi, single-celled motile algae — did not fit cleanly into either kingdom, so more scientific classification systems evolved over time based on cell structure, thallus organisation, mode of nutrition, mode of reproduction, phylogenetic relationships and habitat.

Evolution of Kingdom Systems

Two Kingdom (Linnaeus)

  • Kingdoms: Plantae & Animalia.
  • Based on mobility, mode of nutrition and presence/absence of a cell wall.
  • Drawback: no distinction between prokaryotes/eukaryotes, unicellular/multicellular, or photosynthetic/non-photosynthetic organisms — bacteria, fungi and algae were awkwardly grouped with plants.

Three Kingdom (Haeckel, 1866)

  • Kingdoms: Plantae, Animalia, and a new kingdom Protista to house unicellular organisms not clearly plant or animal.
  • First attempt to separate simple, mostly unicellular forms from complex multicellular plants and animals.

Four Kingdom (Copeland, 1956)

  • Kingdoms: Monera (prokaryotes), Protista, Plantae, Animalia.
  • First system to formally separate the prokaryotic bacteria (Monera) from the eukaryotic Protista, recognising the fundamental cellular divide.

Five Kingdom (R.H. Whittaker, 1969)

  • Kingdoms: Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae, Animalia — the system followed by NCERT.
  • Basis of classification: cell structure (prokaryotic/eukaryotic), body/thallus organisation, mode of nutrition, mode of reproduction, and phylogenetic relationships.
  • First system to give Fungi a separate kingdom, recognising their distinct chitinous cell wall and absorptive (saprophytic) nutrition.

Six Kingdom (Cavalier-Smith, 1998)

  • Kingdoms: Eubacteria, Archaebacteria (or Archaea), Protista, Fungi, Plantae, Animalia.
  • Splits Whittaker's single Monera into two kingdoms because Archaebacteria and Eubacteria differ radically in cell-wall chemistry, membrane lipids and RNA sequences, despite both being prokaryotic.

Three Domains (Carl Woese, 1990)

  • Domains: Bacteria, Archaea, Eukarya — a rank above kingdom, based on comparing ribosomal RNA (rRNA) gene sequences.
  • Shows Archaea are as different from Bacteria as they are from Eukaryotes, so all prokaryotes cannot simply be lumped together phylogenetically.
Figure 5.1: Whittaker's Five Kingdom system, arranged by increasing complexity of body organisation
NEET trap — Kingdom vs Domain: "Domain" (Woese) is a taxonomic rank higher than Kingdom, based purely on rRNA sequence comparison. It splits the prokaryotes into two domains (Bacteria and Archaea) while keeping every eukaryotic kingdom together in a single domain, Eukarya. Do not confuse the three-Domain system with the six-Kingdom system — they use different ranks, though both separate Archaebacteria from Eubacteria.

Kingdom Monera

Monerans are the most primitive and most abundant micro-organisms on Earth. They are found virtually everywhere — from soil and water to hot springs, deep-sea vents, and as symbionts or parasites inside other organisms.

General characters of Monera: Prokaryotic (no nuclear membrane, so no true nucleus — genetic material is a single circular, naked, double-stranded DNA lying free in the cytoplasm as a nucleoid); unicellular; cell wall present in most (peptidoglycan/murein in Eubacteria, absent in Mycoplasma, chemically distinct in Archaebacteria); 70S ribosomes; no membrane-bound organelles (no mitochondria, plastids, ER, Golgi body); reproduce mainly by binary fission; extremely diverse metabolically — this is the only group showing every possible mode of nutrition (autotrophic and heterotrophic, both photosynthetic and chemosynthetic).

Shape of Bacteria

Figure 5.2: The four basic shapes of bacteria. Cocci and bacilli can further occur singly, in pairs (diplo-), chains (strepto-) or clusters (staphylo-).

Bacterial Life Processes

  • Nutrition:
    • Autotrophic — photosynthetic (use bacteriochlorophyll, e.g. purple & green sulfur bacteria) or chemosynthetic (oxidise inorganic substrates for energy, e.g. nitrifying bacteria).
    • Heterotrophic — the vast majority; saprophytic (decomposers), parasitic (pathogens), or symbiotic (e.g. Rhizobium in root nodules).
  • Respiration: aerobic, anaerobic, or facultative anaerobic (can switch depending on oxygen availability).
  • Reproduction:
    • Asexual — binary fission is the primary mode (cell elongates, DNA replicates, and the cell splits into two); under unfavourable conditions some form thick-walled resistant endospores.
    • Sexual recombination — bacteria never fuse gametes; instead genetic material is transferred between cells by three distinct DNA-transfer mechanisms: transformation (uptake of naked DNA from the environment), conjugation (direct DNA transfer through a cytoplasmic bridge/pilus between two cells), and transduction (DNA transfer via a bacteriophage vector).

Economic Importance of Bacteria

  • Beneficial: nitrogen fixation (Rhizobium, Azotobacter) enriching soil fertility; curd/dairy fermentation (Lactobacillus); antibiotic production; retting of fibres (jute, flax); decomposition and nutrient recycling; biogas production by methanogens; genetic engineering (production of insulin, vaccines).
  • Harmful: spoilage of food; plant, animal and human diseases — e.g. typhoid (Salmonella typhi), cholera (Vibrio cholerae), tuberculosis (Mycobacterium tuberculosis), anthrax (Bacillus anthracis), citrus canker.

Archaebacteria vs Eubacteria

Archaebacteria ("ancient bacteria") differ fundamentally from all other bacteria in the chemistry of their cell wall (which lacks peptidoglycan/murein), enabling them to survive in the most extreme habitats on Earth — likely similar to conditions on early Earth.

Archaebacterial groupHabitat / feature
MethanogensFound in marshy/anaerobic areas, and in the gut of ruminant animals (cattle, buffalo) where they produce methane (marsh gas / biogas) from organic matter; responsible for the flatulence of ruminants and are exploited commercially for biogas production.
HalophilesThrive in extremely salty environments — salt lakes, salt pans, the Dead Sea.
ThermoacidophilesThrive in hot, acidic environments such as sulfur springs and hydrothermal vents (e.g. Yellowstone hot springs).

Eubacteria ("true bacteria") are the large, familiar group of bacteria with a rigid cell wall; if motile, they bear one or more flagella. Two economically important eubacterial groups highlighted by NCERT:

Cyanobacteria (blue-green algae)

  • Photosynthetic (chlorophyll a, like plants) — often called blue-green algae, though prokaryotic.
  • Unicellular, colonial, or filamentous; found in fresh water, marine and terrestrial habitats.
  • Cells surrounded by a gelatinous/mucilaginous sheath.
  • Many filamentous forms have specialised thick-walled cells called heterocysts that are the sites of nitrogen fixation, e.g. Nostoc, Anabaena.
  • Form resting spores (akinetes) under unfavourable conditions.

Mycoplasma

  • Completely lack a cell wall — the only bacteria without one.
  • Smallest known living cells and can survive without oxygen.
  • Because they have no rigid wall, they can change shape.
  • Many are pathogenic to plants and animals (e.g. cause several plant diseases).

Kingdom Protista

General characters: All single-celled (unicellular, though some are colonial) eukaryotes are placed in Protista. It is a boundary/link group whose members show characteristics that connect it to the plant, animal and fungal kingdoms — hence Protists are treated as a link connecting other eukaryotic kingdoms. Cell structure is eukaryotic (true nucleus, membrane-bound organelles). They reproduce both asexually and sexually — sexual reproduction occurs by a process involving cell fusion (syngamy) followed by meiosis. Locomotion is via flagella or cilia. Nutrition varies widely: photosynthetic, holozoic (predatory) or saprophytic.

Chrysophytes

Includes diatoms and desmids (golden algae). Found in fresh water and marine environments; mostly photosynthetic. Cell wall of diatoms forms two thin overlapping shells (like a soap box) called frustules, embedded with silica — making the wall indestructible. Because these shells accumulate over millions of years on the ocean floor, they form diatomaceous earth (used in polishing, filtration, insulation). Diatoms are the chief "producers" in the oceans.

Dinoflagellates

Mostly marine and photosynthetic; appear yellow, green, brown, blue or red depending on the main pigments present. Cell wall is stiffened by cellulose plates on the outer surface. Two flagella — one lies longitudinally, the other transversely in a furrow between the wall plates. Rapid multiplication of red-pigmented dinoflagellates (e.g. Gonyaulax) causes the sea to turn red, a phenomenon known as red tide; toxins released can kill large numbers of fish.

Euglenoids

Mostly freshwater organisms found in stagnant water. Instead of a cell wall they have a protein-rich layer called a pellicle, which makes the body flexible. Bear two flagella — one short, one long. Mixotrophic nutrition is the hallmark: in sunlight they photosynthesise (chlorophyll a & b, like plants); in the absence of sunlight they behave as heterotrophs by predating on smaller organisms. E.g. Euglena.

Slime Moulds

Saprophytic, chemoheterotrophic protists. Under favourable conditions they exist as a mass of undifferentiated, moving protoplasm called a plasmodium that grows and engulfs organic matter/food particles as it moves. Under unfavourable conditions, the plasmodium differentiates into fruiting bodies bearing spores at their tips. Spores are extremely resistant and can survive for years, even under adverse conditions, and are dispersed by air currents.

Protozoans — Four Major Groups

All protozoans are heterotrophic and live as predators or parasites; considered to be primitive/simplest forms related to animals.

GroupLocomotory structureKey features & examples
Amoeboid protozoans (Rhizopoda)Pseudopodia ("false feet")Live in fresh water, sea water or moist soil; some marine forms bear silica shells on their surface; some are parasitic, e.g. Entamoeba histolytica (causes amoebic dysentery).
Flagellated protozoansFlagellaFree-living or parasitic; parasitic forms cause serious diseases, e.g. Trypanosoma causes African sleeping sickness, transmitted by the tsetse fly.
Ciliated protozoansCilia (numerous, all over the body)Aquatic, actively moving organisms; have a cavity (gullet) that opens to the outside via a cell mouth (cytostome) through which food is channelled by ciliary movement, e.g. Paramecium.
SporozoansNone (non-motile)Diverse life cycle with an infectious spore-like stage; includes the deadly malarial parasite Plasmodium, which requires two hosts (mosquito and human) to complete its life cycle.

Kingdom Fungi

General characters: Fungi are eukaryotic, achlorophyllous (non-green) heterotrophs. Most are saprophytic (feed on dead organic matter), some are parasitic (live on other living organisms and cause diseases), and some form symbiotic relationships — with algae as lichens and with plant roots as mycorrhiza. The body is a network of long, slender thread-like structures called hyphae; the network of hyphae is termed mycelium. Some hyphae are continuous tubes filled with multinucleated cytoplasm — called coenocytic hyphae; others have cross-walls or septa. The cell wall is made of chitin and polysaccharides (never cellulose). Fungi generally store food reserves as glycogen, not starch.
Reproduction in fungi: occurs by vegetative means (fragmentation, fission and budding), by asexual means (via spores called conidia or sporangiospores or zoospores), and by sexual means (via oospores, ascospores and basidiospores). Sexual reproduction proceeds in three sequential steps: (1) plasmogamy — fusion of protoplasms between two motile or non-motile gametes; (2) karyogamy — fusion of the two nuclei; (3) meiosis in the zygote producing haploid spores. After plasmogamy but before karyogamy, the fungal cell may contain two unfused haploid nuclei (n+n) per cell — this stage is called the dikaryon stage (dikaryophase), and it is unique to fungi.

Classes of Fungi

ClassHabitat & myceliumAsexual reproductionSexual reproductionExamples
PhycomycetesAquatic habitats, on decaying wood, or as obligate parasites on plants; mycelium aseptate & coenocytic.Zoospores (motile) or aplanospores (non-motile), produced endogenously in a sporangium.By fusion of two gametes — isogamous, anisogamous or oogamous — forming a thick-walled zygospore.Mucor, Rhizopus (bread mould), Albugo.
Ascomycetes ("sac fungi")Mostly multicellular (some unicellular, e.g. yeast), saprophytic, decomposers, parasitic or coprophilous (grow on dung); mycelium branched and septate.Conidia produced exogenously on the conidiophores.Fusion of two cells forming ascospores that develop endogenously inside sac-like asci, arranged in fruiting bodies called ascocarps.Aspergillus, Claviceps, Neurospora (used in biochemical/genetic work), Saccharomyces cerevisiae (yeast, used in fermentation).
BasidiomycetesCommon in soil, on logs/tree stumps and as parasites — e.g. rusts and smuts; mycelium branched and septate.Vegetative and asexual spores generally absent.Fusion of two somatic/vegetative cells of different strains/genotypes gives rise to a dikaryotic mycelium bearing basidiospores exogenously on a basidium; fruiting bodies are called basidiocarps (the visible mushroom).Mushrooms, bracket fungi, puffballs, Ustilago (smut), Puccinia (rust).
Deuteromycetes ("Fungi Imperfecti")Saprophytes or parasites; mycelium septate and branched.Only known method of reproduction — conidia.Not yet observed for these fungi. As soon as the sexual (perfect) stage of a Deuteromycete is discovered, it is immediately moved into the appropriate class (Ascomycetes or Basidiomycetes).Alternaria, Trichoderma, Colletotrichum.

Lichens

A symbiotic (mutualistic) association between an alga and a fungus. The algal component (phycobiont) is autotrophic and manufactures food for the fungus through photosynthesis; the fungal component (mycobiont) provides shelter and absorbs water and mineral nutrients for the alga. Lichens are extremely sensitive to air/sulphur-dioxide pollution and are therefore used as reliable pollution indicators.

Mycorrhiza

A symbiotic association between fungi and the roots of higher (vascular) plants. The fungus vastly increases the effective surface area for water and mineral absorption for the plant, while receiving organic nutrients/food manufactured by the plant in return. Many gymnosperm/forest trees depend heavily on mycorrhizal associations for normal growth.

Viruses & Sub-viral Agents

Viruses are non-cellular, obligate intracellular parasites — they show no signs of life (no metabolism, no growth) outside a living host cell, yet once inside a host they take over its cellular machinery to replicate. This dual nature places them at the boundary between living and non-living.

Discovery timeline:
  • D.J. Ivanowsky (1892) — recognised that the sap of a tobacco plant infected with mosaic disease contained a disease-causing agent smaller than bacteria, since it passed through a bacteria-proof (Chamberland) filter; he still believed it might be a toxin.
  • M.W. Beijerinck (1898) — showed that the fluid from the infected tobacco leaf, after passing through the filter, could still cause infection when applied to a healthy plant, and named it Contagium vivum fluidum ("contagious living fluid") — establishing its infectious nature.
  • W.M. Stanley (1935) — demonstrated that viruses could be crystallised, and that these crystals consist largely of protein (with nucleic acid), confirming the particulate, non-cellular nature of viruses.

Structural Components

Every virus has a core of nucleic acid — either DNA or RNA, never both — surrounded by a protein coat called the capsid, made of small subunits called capsomeres. Plant viruses mostly carry single-stranded RNA; animal viruses may carry single- or double-stranded RNA or DNA; bacteriophages (bacteria-infecting viruses) are usually double-stranded DNA viruses.

Figure 5.3: Two classic virus body plans — helical symmetry (TMV) vs a head-and-tail bacteriophage

Viruses can only replicate inside a living host cell, entirely hijacking the host's ribosomes, enzymes and raw materials to synthesise their own nucleic acid and protein coat. Viral diseases in plants include mosaic disease and leaf curl (transmitted via sap-sucking insects, seeds and vegetative propagules); in humans and animals, viruses cause mumps, smallpox, herpes, influenza, common cold, and AIDS.

Sub-viral Infectious Agents

AgentCompositionDiscovered byKey point
ViroidsFree RNA only — no protein coat at all.T.O. Diener (1971)The RNA of a viroid is of low molecular weight compared to viruses; causes the potato spindle tuber disease.
VirusoidsSmall circular RNA encapsidated inside the protein coat of a "helper" virus.—Cannot replicate independently; depends entirely on the co-infecting helper virus.
PrionsAbnormally folded protein only — no nucleic acid at all.Stanley PrusinerInfectious protein particles resembling viruses in size; cause serious neurodegenerative diseases such as Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease (CJD) in humans and "mad cow disease" (bovine spongiform encephalopathy) in cattle.
NEET trap: Viroids differ from viruses mainly in lacking a protein coat, while prions are unique in being purely proteinaceous infectious agents that completely lack nucleic acid — the exact opposite composition to a viroid. Remember: Virus = nucleic acid + protein coat; Viroid = RNA only; Prion = protein only.

Ch 1 Some Basic Concepts of Chemistry — Mole Concept & Stoichiometry

Chemistry is fundamentally a quantitative science — reactions occur between fixed numbers of particles, not fixed masses "by feel." The mole concept is the bridge that lets us convert between the invisible world of atoms/molecules and the measurable world of grams and litres in the lab. Nearly every numerical NEET question — from stoichiometry to solutions to electrochemistry — ultimately reduces to this chapter's tools.

1. Laws of Chemical Combination & Dalton's Atomic Theory

Before atoms could be counted, 18th–19th century chemists established these empirical laws purely from careful weighing experiments:

LawStatement
Law of Conservation of Mass (Lavoisier, 1789)Mass can neither be created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction — total mass of reactants = total mass of products.
Law of Definite (Constant) Proportions (Proust, 1799)A given pure chemical compound always contains the same elements combined in a fixed ratio by mass, regardless of source or method of preparation — e.g. water is always 1:8 H:O by mass.
Law of Multiple Proportions (Dalton, 1803)When two elements combine to form more than one compound, the masses of one element that combine with a fixed mass of the other are in a ratio of small whole numbers — e.g. C combines with O to form CO (mass ratio C:O = 12:16) and CO₂ (12:32); for fixed 12 g C, O masses are 16 and 32 — ratio 1:2.
Gay Lussac's Law of Gaseous Volumes (1808)When gases react, the volumes of reactants and products (at the same temperature and pressure) are in a ratio of small whole numbers — e.g. H₂ + Cl₂ → 2HCl is a 1:1:2 volume ratio.
Avogadro's Law (1811)Equal volumes of all gases, at the same temperature and pressure, contain equal numbers of molecules — this resolved the contradiction between Dalton's theory (indivisible atoms) and Gay Lussac's law by introducing the idea of diatomic molecules (e.g. H₂, not H).
Dalton's Atomic Theory (1808) — core postulates: matter consists of indivisible atoms; atoms of the same element are identical in mass and properties, atoms of different elements differ; atoms combine in simple whole-number ratios to form compounds; atoms can neither be created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction (only rearranged).
Advanced Insight — Where Dalton's Theory Breaks Down
  • "Atoms are indivisible" fails at the level of nuclear reactions and the existence of subatomic particles (electron, proton, neutron) — atoms are divisible, just not by ordinary chemical means.
  • "Atoms of the same element are identical in mass" fails for isotopes (same atomic number, different mass number, e.g. ¹²C and ¹⁴C) — discovered decades after Dalton.
  • "Atoms of different elements differ in mass/properties" fails for isobars (different elements, same mass number, e.g. ⁴⁰Ar and ⁴⁰Ca can have very similar mass).
  • Conservation of mass is only approximately true — Einstein's mass–energy equivalence (E = mc²) shows a tiny mass change accompanies the energy released/absorbed in any reaction, though it is undetectably small for ordinary chemical reactions (only significant in nuclear reactions).
NEET Exam Traps
  • Do not confuse Law of Definite Proportions (one compound, fixed ratio) with Law of Multiple Proportions (same two elements, multiple compounds, whole-number ratio between the ratios) — a very commonly swapped pair in MCQs.
  • Avogadro's Law applies only to gases (and only under identical T, P) — it says nothing about liquids or solids.
  • Non-stoichiometric compounds (e.g. Fe₀.₉₅O) genuinely violate the Law of Definite Proportions in the strict sense — a known exception sometimes tested at higher difficulty.

2. Atomic Mass, Molecular Mass & the Mole

Atomic mass is expressed in atomic mass units (u), defined as exactly 1/12th the mass of one atom of the ¹²C isotope (the modern reference standard, adopted 1961). The mole is the SI unit for "amount of substance" — 1 mole of any species contains a fixed number of elementary entities, the Avogadro constant, chosen so that 1 mole of ¹²C atoms has a mass of exactly 12 g.

QuantitySymbol / Value
Avogadro's NumberNₐ = 6.022 × 10²³ /mol
Molar Volume (Old STP: 273.15 K, 1 atm)22.4 L/mol
Molar Volume (New IUPAC STP: 273.15 K, 1 bar)22.7 L/mol
Molar Volume (NTP: 298.15 K, 1 atm)≈ 24.45 L/mol
Mass of Electron9.1 × 10⁻³¹ kg (≈ 1/1837 u)
Mass of Proton1.673 × 10⁻²⁷ kg (≈ 1 u)
Mass of Neutron1.675 × 10⁻²⁷ kg (≈ 1 u)
Advanced Insight — Average Atomic Mass & Isotopic Abundance

The atomic mass quoted on the periodic table is a weighted average over all naturally occurring isotopes, weighted by their fractional abundance: Average atomic mass = Σ(isotopic mass × fractional abundance). E.g. chlorine's atomic mass of 35.5 u arises from ~75% ³⁵Cl and ~25% ³⁷Cl — this weighted-average calculation is a very common NEET numerical.

Gram atomic mass = atomic mass expressed in grams (mass of 1 mole of atoms); gram molecular mass = molecular mass expressed in grams (mass of 1 mole of molecules); gram equivalent mass = equivalent mass expressed in grams — three related but distinct quantities that are frequently confused.

NEET Exam Traps
  • "Molecular mass" applies strictly to substances that exist as discrete molecules (H₂O, CO₂); for ionic/network solids like NaCl or SiO₂, the correct term is formula mass (no true "molecule" exists) — examiners sometimes test this terminology distinction.
  • 1 mole always means 6.022 × 10²³ entities of whatever is specified — 1 mole of electrons, 1 mole of Na⁺ ions, and 1 mole of NaCl "formula units" are all valid, but have very different masses; always check what the question is asking moles OF.
  • Do not round Avogadro's number or molar volume mid-calculation in multi-step numericals — small rounding errors compound and can shift the final answer to a wrong MCQ option (a classic distractor-design trick).

3. Mole–Mass–Particle–Volume Relationships

Four interconvertible routes to find the number of moles (n) of a substance — this diagram is the single most useful mental model for the whole chapter:

From Mass:
n = Given Mass (g) / Molar Mass (g/mol)
From Particles:
n = No. of Particles / Nₐ
From Gas Volume (STP):
n = Volume (L) / Molar Volume
Reverse conversions:
Mass = n × M  |  Particles = n × Nₐ
Advanced Insight — Counting Constituent Particles, Not Just Formula Units

A frequent higher-order NEET question asks for the number of a specific type of particle inside a compound, not just the number of formula units — e.g. moles of oxygen ATOMS in 2 mol of Al₂(SO₄)₃ requires multiplying by the number of O atoms per formula unit (12), giving 24 mol O atoms, i.e. 24 × Nₐ atoms. Always multiply mol of compound by the subscript of the atom/ion of interest before converting to particle count.

Similarly, for ionic compounds, "moles of ions" ≠ "moles of formula units" — 1 mol of Al₂(SO₄)₃ gives 2 mol Al³⁺ and 3 mol SO₄²⁻ on complete dissociation (5 mol of ions total), which matters heavily in colligative-properties and van't Hoff factor questions later in the syllabus.

Vapour Density (V.D.): a gas's density relative to hydrogen gas under identical conditions — always exactly half its molar mass, since M(H₂) = 2 g/mol.

Vapour Density = Molar Mass / 2   ⟹   Molar Mass = 2 × V.D.

NEET Exam Traps
  • The 22.4 L/mol (or 22.7 L/mol) molar volume applies ONLY to gases at STP — never apply it to liquids, solids, or gases at non-standard conditions (use the ideal gas equation PV = nRT instead for those).
  • Vapour density is a pure number (no units) since it's a ratio of densities — do not attach g/L or similar units to it in an answer.
  • When a question gives volume "at STP" vs "at NTP" vs "at room temperature," using the wrong molar volume value is one of the most common silent errors in mole-concept numericals.

4. Percentage Composition, Empirical & Molecular Formula

Mass Percentage of an Element in a compound:

% Element = (Mass of element in molecule / Molar mass of compound) × 100

Minimum Molecular Mass (assuming at least 1 atom of the element is present — used for macromolecules/proteins where exact composition is unknown):

Min. Molecular Mass = (100 × Atomic Mass) / % of Element

Empirical Formula (EF) gives the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms of each element in a compound. Molecular Formula (MF) gives the actual number of atoms of each element in one molecule. MF is always a whole-number multiple (n) of EF: MF = n × EF, where n = Molecular Mass / Empirical Formula Mass.

StepProcedure
1Convert given mass % (or mass) of each element to moles by dividing by its atomic mass.
2Divide each element's mole value by the smallest mole value obtained, to get a simple ratio.
3If the ratio is not a whole number, multiply all values by the smallest integer that makes them whole (e.g. ×2 for a value of 1.5, ×3 for 1.33 or 0.33).
4Write the empirical formula using these whole-number subscripts; calculate empirical formula mass.
5Find n = (given molecular mass) / (empirical formula mass); multiply all EF subscripts by n to get the molecular formula.
Worked Example: A compound contains 40% C, 6.7% H, 53.3% O by mass, with molecular mass 180 g/mol.
Moles: C = 40/12 = 3.33, H = 6.7/1 = 6.7, O = 53.3/16 = 3.33
Divide by smallest (3.33): C = 1, H = 2, O = 1 → Empirical formula CH₂O (mass = 30)
n = 180/30 = 6 → Molecular formula = C₆H₁₂O₆ (glucose)
Advanced Insight — Combustion Analysis

For organic compounds, empirical formula is classically found via combustion analysis: a known mass of sample is completely burnt in excess O₂, and the CO₂ and H₂O produced are trapped and weighed separately (CO₂ in KOH/soda-lime, H₂O in anhydrous CaCl₂/Mg(ClO₄)₂). All the carbon in the sample converts to CO₂ and all the hydrogen converts to H₂O, so: mass of C = mass of CO₂ × (12/44); mass of H = mass of H₂O × (2/18). Any oxygen (or other element) present is usually found by difference: mass of O = total sample mass − (mass of C + mass of H + mass of any other analysed element).

NEET Exam Traps
  • Never round mole ratios too early — 1.33 should be recognised as 4/3 (multiply by 3), not carelessly rounded to 1; common "near-whole-number" ratios to memorise: 1.5→×2, 1.33/0.33→×3, 1.25/0.75→×4, 1.2/0.8→×5.
  • Empirical formula and molecular formula are identical (n = 1) for many small molecules like H₂O and CO₂, but this is NOT true in general — always verify with the given molecular mass before assuming they're the same.
  • Compounds with the same empirical formula can be entirely different substances — e.g. CH₂O is both the EF of glucose (C₆H₁₂O₆) and the MF of formaldehyde itself; EF alone never uniquely identifies a compound.

5. Stoichiometry & Limiting Reagent

In a balanced reaction, the limiting reagent is the reactant that runs out first, stopping the reaction and capping the amount of product formed; the other reactant(s) are said to be "in excess." To identify it, divide each reactant's given moles by its own stoichiometric coefficient — the smallest ratio wins (that reactant is limiting).

Worked Example: Combustion of methane — CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O
Given: 2.0 mol CH₄ and 3.0 mol O₂
Ratio(CH₄) = 2.0 / 1 = 2.0  |  Ratio(O₂) = 3.0 / 2 = 1.5
Since 1.5 < 2.0, O₂ is the limiting reagent; CH₄ is in excess.
Moles of CO₂ formed = 1 × 1.5 = 1.5 mol  |  Moles of H₂O formed = 2 × 1.5 = 3.0 mol
Advanced Insight — Finding Leftover Excess Reagent

Once the limiting reagent is identified, the moles of excess reagent actually CONSUMED = (moles of limiting reagent) × (stoichiometric coefficient of excess reagent / stoichiometric coefficient of limiting reagent). Moles of excess reagent REMAINING = initial moles − moles consumed. In the worked example above: O₂ consumed = 2.0 × (2/1) = 4.0 mol — but only 3.0 mol O₂ was given, confirming O₂ is indeed limiting (cannot consume more than what's available); CH₄ consumed = 1.5 × (1/2) = 0.75 mol, so CH₄ remaining = 2.0 − 0.75 = 1.25 mol left over.

For reactions involving three or more reactants, the same "divide by coefficient, smallest wins" rule extends directly — just compare all the ratios together rather than pairwise.

NEET Exam Traps
  • Never compare raw given moles directly to decide the limiting reagent unless all stoichiometric coefficients are equal — always divide by the coefficient first; comparing raw moles is the single most common stoichiometry error.
  • Product amount in ANY multi-step calculation must always be based on the limiting reagent alone — using the excess reagent's moles instead gives an answer that is too high.
  • Always double-check the equation is correctly balanced before starting mole-ratio calculations — an unbalanced equation invalidates every subsequent step.

6. Concentration Terms for Solutions

These are the standard ways of expressing "how much solute in how much solution/solvent" — essential groundwork for the later Solutions chapter and repeatedly tested directly here too.

TermFormulaNotes
Molarity (M)M = moles of solute / volume of solution (L)Most commonly used; changes with temperature since volume expands/contracts on heating/cooling.
Molality (m)m = moles of solute / mass of solvent (kg)Temperature-independent (based on mass, not volume) — preferred for precise/colligative-property work.
Mole Fraction (x)xᵢ = moles of component i / total moles of all componentsDimensionless; sum of mole fractions of all components in a solution always equals 1.
Mass Percentage (w/w %)% = (mass of solute / mass of solution) × 100Independent of temperature.
Volume Percentage (v/v %)% = (volume of solute / volume of solution) × 100Common for liquid-in-liquid solutions, e.g. alcohol content.
Normality (N)N = moles of equivalents of solute / volume of solution (L)N = M × n-factor (n-factor = basicity for acids, acidity for bases, |charge × number of ions| for salts, electrons transferred for redox species).
Parts Per Million (ppm)ppm = (mass of solute / mass of solution) × 10⁶Used for trace quantities, e.g. pollutant or water-hardness concentrations.
Advanced Insight — Relating Molarity & Molality via Density

Molarity and molality can be interconverted if the solution's density (d, in g/mL) and the solute's molar mass (M₀) are known:

Molarity = (1000 × d × m) / (1000 + m × M₀)

where m is molality. This formula is a favourite higher-difficulty NEET numerical since it links three concentration systems (molarity, molality, density) in one equation — memorising its derivation logic (mass of solution = mass of solvent + mass of solute, then converting mass of solution to volume via density) is more reliable than memorising the formula alone.

Dilution law: M₁V₁ = M₂V₂ (moles of solute unchanged on dilution) — extremely high-frequency in numericals; note this only holds for molarity/normality (volume-based terms), never for molality or mole fraction directly.

NEET Exam Traps
  • Molarity changes with temperature (volume expands on heating, so M decreases slightly) while molality, mole fraction, and mass % do NOT — a frequently tested conceptual distinction.
  • "Volume of solution" in molarity is NOT the same as "volume of solvent added" — mixing solute and solvent does not give perfectly additive volumes in general (though this approximation is often used for dilute aqueous solutions).
  • n-factor is reaction-dependent for polyprotic acids/bases and redox species — e.g. H₃PO₄ can have n-factor 1, 2, or 3 depending on how many H⁺ actually react in that specific reaction, not always its total basicity.

7. Purity & Percentage Yield

Percentage Purity:
% Purity = (Pure Mass / Sample Mass) × 100
Pure Mass from Sample:
Pure Mass = Sample Mass × (Purity % / 100)
Percentage Yield: how efficient a reaction actually is, compared to the maximum possible (theoretical) yield calculated purely from stoichiometry.
% Yield = (Actual Yield / Theoretical Yield) × 100
NEET Exam Traps
  • Theoretical yield must always be calculated from the LIMITING reagent, never the reagent in excess — a very common compounding error when purity/yield questions are combined with a limiting-reagent step.
  • Percentage yield can never legitimately exceed 100% for a single, correctly-analysed reaction — an answer above 100% signals either a calculation error or (in rare real lab cases) impure/wet product being weighed.
  • "Impure sample mass" and "pure substance mass" are different quantities — always re-read which one a question is asking you to find or has given you before plugging into a stoichiometry step.

Chapter 2 topics

Ch 2 Structure of Atom

The atom was once thought to be the smallest, indivisible particle of matter. Discoveries between 1897 and 1932 revealed that the atom itself is built from smaller subatomic particles — the electron, proton and neutron — and that these particles are arranged in a very specific way that determines how each element behaves chemically.

1. Discovery of Subatomic Particles

Three key experiments established that atoms are made of charged and neutral particles:

Electron — J.J. Thomson (1897)
Cathode ray tube experiment. Rays travelled from cathode to anode, were deflected by electric/magnetic fields toward the positive plate, proving they were negatively charged particles present in all matter.
Proton — E. Goldstein (1886)
Discovered canal rays (anode rays) in a perforated-cathode discharge tube — positively charged particles whose mass depended on the gas used.
Neutron — J. Chadwick (1932)
Bombarded beryllium with alpha particles and detected a neutral particle of mass nearly equal to the proton — the last fundamental particle to be discovered.
Nucleus — Rutherford (1911)
Gold foil (alpha-scattering) experiment showed almost all mass and positive charge is concentrated in a tiny central nucleus.
ParticleSymbolChargeMass (kg)Relative Mass
Electrone⁻−1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C9.1 × 10⁻³¹1/1837 (≈0)
Protonp⁺+1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C1.672 × 10⁻²⁷1
Neutronn0 (neutral)1.675 × 10⁻²⁷1
Charge-to-mass ratio (e/m) & Charge on the Electron
  • Thomson determined the e/m ratio of the electron from cathode ray deflection in electric and magnetic fields: e/m = 1.758820 × 10¹¹ C/kg.
  • Millikan's Oil Drop Experiment (1909) measured the actual charge on the electron: e = −1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. Combining this with Thomson's e/m ratio gives the electron's mass, 9.1 × 10⁻³¹ kg.

Atomic Number, Mass Number, Isotopes & Isobars

The number of protons in the nucleus of an atom is its atomic number (Z) — it uniquely identifies the element, since in a neutral atom the number of electrons equals the number of protons. The mass number (A) is the total count of protons and neutrons (collectively called nucleons) in the nucleus: A = Z + n (number of neutrons). An atom of an element X is represented as AₖZX.

TermDefinitionExample
IsotopesSame atomic number (Z), different mass number (A) — same element, differ in number of neutrons; identical chemical properties, slightly different physical properties¹H, ²H (Deuterium), ³H (Tritium); ¹²C, ¹³C, ¹⁴C
IsobarsSame mass number (A), different atomic number (Z) — different elements that happen to have equal total nucleon count¹⁴C and ¹⁴N; ⁴⁰Ar, ⁴⁰K and ⁴⁰Ca
IsotonesSame number of neutrons (A − Z), different atomic and mass numbers (an extra term sometimes tested)³⁰Si and ³¹P (both have 16 neutrons)
Figure 2.0: The three isotopes of hydrogen — identical atomic number (1 proton), increasing mass number as neutrons are added. Blue dot = orbiting electron.

2. Evolution of Atomic Models

Figure 2.1: Evolution from Thomson's uniform sphere of charge, to Rutherford's tiny dense nucleus with electrons orbiting in empty space, to Bohr's fixed circular energy shells.
Thomson's Model: Positive charge spread uniformly through a sphere, with electrons embedded like seeds — explained overall neutrality but could not explain scattering results.
Rutherford's Model: A small, dense, positively-charged nucleus at the centre; electrons revolve around it in circular orbits; most of the atom is empty space. Could not explain why revolving electrons don't spiral into the nucleus (a violation of classical electrodynamics).
Alpha-Scattering Observations & Their Conclusions
  • Most α-particles passed straight through the gold foil → atom is mostly empty space.
  • A few were deflected at small angles → a concentrated positive charge exists.
  • Very few (~1 in 8000) bounced straight back → the nucleus is extremely small and dense.

3. Electromagnetic Radiation & Planck's Quantum Theory

Light and other forms of radiant energy travel through space as electromagnetic (EM) waves — oscillating electric and magnetic fields perpendicular to each other and to the direction of propagation, requiring no medium. All EM waves travel at the speed of light, c = 3 × 10⁸ m/s, related to wavelength (λ) and frequency (ν) by c = νλ. Wavenumber, ῡ = 1/λ, is the number of wavelengths per unit length.

Planck's Quantum Theory (1900):
  • Energy is emitted or absorbed by matter only in discrete packets called quanta (for light, called photons), not continuously.
  • The energy of one quantum is directly proportional to its frequency: E = hν = hc/λ, where h = Planck's constant = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s.
  • Total energy transferred is an integral multiple of hν: E = nhν (n = 1, 2, 3…).
  • This theory successfully explained black-body radiation, a phenomenon classical physics could not account for.
Photoelectric Effect (Einstein, 1905):

When light of sufficiently high frequency strikes a metal surface, electrons are ejected instantly — called photoelectrons. Key experimental observations, all explained by treating light as a stream of photons:

  • Electron ejection begins only above a minimum frequency, the threshold frequency (ν₀), characteristic of the metal — no ejection occurs below it, however intense the light.
  • Kinetic energy of ejected electrons increases linearly with frequency of light, but is independent of its intensity.
  • Number of electrons ejected (photoelectric current) depends on the intensity of light, not its frequency.
  • Einstein's photoelectric equation: hν = hν₀ + ½mv² i.e. (energy of incident photon) = (work function, W₀) + (kinetic energy of ejected electron).
Figure 2.0b: The photoelectric effect — a photon of energy hν strikes the metal; if hν ≥ work function (hν₀), an electron is instantly ejected with kinetic energy hν − hν₀.

Dual behaviour of electromagnetic radiation: phenomena like diffraction and interference are explained only by treating light as a wave, while the photoelectric effect can be explained only by treating light as made of particles (photons). Light — and, as de Broglie later showed, matter too — therefore exhibits wave–particle duality: it shows both wave and particle-like properties depending on the experiment.

Emission and Absorption Spectra

When radiation from a source is passed through a prism, it splits into its component wavelengths — the resulting pattern is a spectrum. An emission spectrum is produced when radiation emitted by an excited atom/substance is passed through a prism (appears as bright coloured lines on a dark background); an absorption spectrum is obtained when white light is passed through a substance first, and the wavelengths absorbed appear as dark lines against a bright, continuous background — the dark lines of an absorption spectrum exactly match the positions of the bright lines of the corresponding emission spectrum.

Line spectrum of hydrogen: Hydrogen gives a line (not continuous) emission spectrum, since only certain specific frequencies of light are emitted, corresponding to electron transitions between fixed energy levels. These lines fall into series, each named after its discoverer:

SeriesTransition (to nₗ)Spectral Region
Lymann → 1Ultraviolet
Balmern → 2Visible
Paschenn → 3Infrared
Brackettn → 4Infrared
Pfundn → 5Infrared

Rydberg's formula gives the wavenumber of each line: ῡ = RH[1/n₁² − 1/n₂²], where RH (Rydberg constant) = 109,677 cm⁻¹, and n₂ > n₁.

Figure 2.0c: Hydrogen atom energy-level diagram — downward arrows show electron transitions that produce the Lyman, Balmer and Paschen spectral series. Energy gap decreases as n increases, so lines converge near n=∞.

4. Bohr's Model of the Atom

Bohr proposed that electrons revolve only in certain fixed circular paths called orbits / energy shells (numbered n = 1, 2, 3… or K, L, M, N…), each with a fixed, quantized energy. As long as an electron stays in one orbit, it does not radiate energy.

Key Postulates:
  • Angular momentum of the electron is quantized: mvr = nh / 2π
  • Energy is absorbed or emitted only when an electron jumps between orbits, as a photon of energy ΔE = E₂ − E₁ = hν.
QuantityFormula (for H-like species, Z = atomic number)
Radius of nth orbitrₙ = 0.529 × (n² / Z) Å
Energy of nth orbitEₙ = −13.6 × (Z² / n²) eV
Velocity of electronvₙ = 2.18 × 10⁶ × (Z / n) m/s

Bohr's model explained the hydrogen line spectrum (Lyman, Balmer, Paschen series) very well, but failed for multi-electron atoms and could not explain the splitting of spectral lines in a magnetic field (Zeeman effect) — limitations that led to the quantum mechanical model.

5. Dual Nature of Matter, Heisenberg's Uncertainty Principle & Quantum Numbers

Reasons for the failure of the Bohr model: it could not explain the spectra of multi-electron atoms, the splitting of spectral lines in a magnetic field (Zeeman effect) or electric field (Stark effect), and it violated the (later-discovered) de Broglie and Heisenberg principles by assuming an electron follows a well-defined circular path.

de Broglie's Dual Behaviour of Matter (1924):

Just as light shows both wave and particle nature, de Broglie proposed that all moving matter — electrons included — has an associated wavelength: λ = h/mv = h/p (p = momentum). This "matter wave" nature was experimentally confirmed for electrons (Davisson–Germer experiment, electron diffraction) and is significant only for particles of very small mass, like electrons — it is undetectable for macroscopic objects.

Heisenberg's Uncertainty Principle (1927):

It is impossible to simultaneously determine, with absolute precision, both the exact position and exact momentum (or velocity) of a microscopic particle like an electron: Δx · Δp ≥ h/4π. The more precisely one quantity is known, the less precisely the other can be known.

Significance: This principle rules out the very idea of a fixed, well-defined orbit/path for an electron (as Bohr proposed) — since to define a path we'd need to know both position and velocity precisely at every instant. It applies negligibly to large (macroscopic) objects, which is why it doesn't affect everyday mechanics, but is critical for sub-atomic particles.

These two principles led to a new, purely probabilistic model — quantum mechanics — developed by Schrödinger, Heisenberg and others. Schrödinger's wave equation, Ĥψ = Eψ, when solved for the hydrogen atom, gives permitted energy levels and corresponding wave functions (ψ). Each solution ψ is called an atomic orbital — a three-dimensional region of space around the nucleus where the probability of finding an electron (given by ψ², the probability density) is maximum, replacing Bohr's fixed circular orbits with a probabilistic electron cloud. Every electron in an atom is uniquely described by four quantum numbers:

Quantum NumberSymbolDescribesValues
PrincipalnShell / size & energy of orbital1, 2, 3…
Azimuthal (Angular)lSubshell / shape of orbital0 to (n−1); e.g. 0=s, 1=p, 2=d, 3=f
MagneticmₗOrientation of orbital in space−l to +l (including 0)
SpinmₛSpin direction of electron+1/2 or −1/2

6. Filling of Orbitals — Rules for Electronic Configuration

Energies of atomic orbitals: In a hydrogen atom (single electron), orbital energy depends only on n (1s = 2s = 2p in energy). In multi-electron atoms, electron–electron repulsions cause orbitals within the same shell to split in energy depending on the subshell too, giving the order 1s < 2s < 2p < 3s < 3p < 4s < 3d… — this is captured by the (n + l) rule below.

Aufbau Principle: Orbitals are filled in order of increasing energy — follow the (n + l) rule; if two orbitals have the same (n + l), the one with lower n is filled first.
Pauli Exclusion Principle: No two electrons in the same atom can have all four quantum numbers identical — an orbital holds a maximum of 2 electrons with opposite spins.
Hund's Rule of Maximum Multiplicity: Electrons occupy degenerate orbitals (of the same subshell) singly first, with parallel spins, before any orbital gets a second electron.
Figure 2.2: Sequence in which subshells are filled with electrons (Aufbau order).
Causes of Stability of Completely-Filled and Half-Filled Subshells

Configurations with fully-filled (e.g. s², p⁶, d¹⁰, f¹⁴) or exactly half-filled (e.g. s¹, p³, d⁵, f⁷) subshells are unusually stable, due to two effects:

  • Symmetrical distribution of electrons: a fully or half-filled subshell has a perfectly symmetric charge distribution, which lowers the overall energy of the atom.
  • Exchange energy: electrons with parallel spins in degenerate orbitals of the same subshell can exchange positions; the more such possible exchanges, the greater the stabilisation (exchange energy) released — half-filled and fully-filled subshells have the maximum number of such exchanges among electrons of the same spin.

This is why Chromium and Copper show exceptional (irregular) configurations, gaining extra stability by "borrowing" one electron from the 4s to complete/half-fill the 3d subshell:

ElementExpected ConfigurationActual (Stable) Configuration
Chromium (Z=24)[Ar] 3d⁴ 4s²[Ar] 3d⁵ 4s¹ (half-filled d, more stable)
Copper (Z=29)[Ar] 3d⁹ 4s²[Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s¹ (fully-filled d, more stable)

7. Shapes of Atomic Orbitals

Figure 2.3: Approximate boundary-surface shapes of s, p and d orbitals. s = 1 orientation, p = 3 orientations (pₓ, p_y, p_z), d = 5 orientations.
Node: A region where the probability of finding an electron is zero. Radial nodes = n − l − 1; Angular nodes = l; Total nodes = n − 1.
Chapter 3 topics

Ch 3 Classification of Elements & Periodicity in Properties

With over 100 known elements, chemists needed a system to organise them so that elements with similar properties could be studied together. The modern Periodic Table arranges all elements in order of increasing atomic number, revealing a repeating ("periodic") pattern in their physical and chemical properties.

1. Historical Attempts at Classification

Figure 3.1: Timeline of periodic classification attempts leading to the modern periodic table.
Döbereiner's Triads (1829): Groups of 3 elements with similar properties where the atomic mass of the middle element ≈ average of the other two (e.g. Li, Na, K).
Newlands' Octaves (1866): Arranged elements by increasing atomic mass; every 8th element had similar properties, like musical notes. Worked only up to calcium.
Mendeleev's Periodic Table (1869): Arranged elements in order of increasing atomic mass into rows (periods) and columns (groups); left gaps for undiscovered elements and successfully predicted their properties.
Moseley's Modern Periodic Law (1913): Properties of elements are a periodic function of their atomic number (not atomic mass) — the basis of today's periodic table.

2. The Modern Long-Form Periodic Table

The modern periodic table has 18 vertical columns (groups) and 7 horizontal rows (periods). Elements in the same group have the same number of valence electrons and hence similar chemical properties; elements in the same period have the same number of shells.

PeriodNumber of ElementsShells Being Filled
121s
282s, 2p
383s, 3p
4184s, 3d, 4p
5185s, 4d, 5p
6326s, 4f, 5d, 6p
