3. Classification into s, p, d, f Blocks

Figure 3.2: Location of the s, p and d blocks within the periodic table (last electron enters s, p, or d subshell respectively). The f-block (lanthanides & actinides, 14 elements each) is placed separately below the main table.
s-block: Groups 1 & 2 (alkali & alkaline earth metals) — last electron enters an s-orbital. Highly reactive, soft metals.
p-block: Groups 13-18 — last electron enters a p-orbital. Contains metals, non-metals, metalloids and noble gases.
d-block: Groups 3-12 (transition elements) — last electron enters a (n−1)d orbital. Show variable oxidation states, form coloured ions.
f-block: Lanthanides (Ce-Lu) & Actinides (Th-Lr) — last electron enters an (n−2)f orbital. Placed separately at the bottom of the table.

4. Periodic Trends in Properties

Figure 3.3: Summary of how key atomic properties change across a period (left → right) and down a group (top → bottom).
PropertyAcross a Period (L→R)Down a GroupReason
Atomic RadiusDecreasesIncreasesIncreasing nuclear charge pulls electrons in; new shells added down the group
Ionization EnthalpyIncreasesDecreasesSmaller size & higher nuclear charge hold outer electron tighter across a period
Electron Gain EnthalpyBecomes more negativeBecomes less negativeGreater tendency to attract an extra electron with smaller size / higher charge
ElectronegativityIncreasesDecreasesStronger pull on shared electron pair in a bond as size decreases
Metallic CharacterDecreasesIncreasesTendency to lose electrons falls across a period, rises down a group

5. Exceptions & Nomenclature of New Elements

Common Exceptions to Remember
  • Ionization enthalpy of Be > B and N > O (extra stability of fully-filled and half-filled subshells).
  • Electron gain enthalpy of Cl is more negative than F — fluorine's very small size causes strong inter-electron repulsion in its compact 2p subshell.
  • Noble gases have the largest atomic radii in their period (measured as van der Waals radius, a different basis than covalent radius used for other elements).

For elements with atomic number > 100 that are newly synthesised, IUPAC nomenclature uses Latin/Greek numerical roots until a permanent name is approved:

Digit0123456789
Rootnilunbitriquadpenthexseptoctenn

Example: Element 118 → "un-un-oct-ium" (Uuo), later officially named Oganesson (Og).

Chapter 4 topics

Ch 4 Chemical Bonding & Molecular Structure

Atoms rarely exist alone — they combine to attain a more stable, lower-energy state, usually by acquiring a noble-gas-like electronic configuration. The force holding atoms together in this combined state is a chemical bond. This is one of the highest-yield NEET chapters — it is tested both directly (shapes, hybridisation, bond order) and indirectly through every other chapter in organic and inorganic chemistry.

1. Kössel–Lewis Approach & the Octet Rule

Kössel and Lewis (1916) explained bond formation in terms of the tendency of atoms to achieve the stable electronic configuration of the nearest noble gas — usually eight electrons in the valence shell (octet rule), except H, Li, Be, B which are satisfied with 2 (duplet) or fewer.

Kössel's contribution: Explained ionic bond formation — electropositive atoms lose electrons to form cations, electronegative atoms gain electrons to form anions; oppositely charged ions attract electrostatically.
Lewis's contribution: Introduced Lewis dot symbols, where valence electrons are shown as dots around the element symbol, and proposed that a covalent bond forms when two atoms share an electron pair so both attain octets.

Steps to draw a Lewis structure:

StepRule
1Count total valence electrons of all atoms (add 1 per negative charge, subtract 1 per positive charge for ions).
2Identify the central atom — usually the least electronegative atom (never H, which is always terminal).
3Connect atoms with single bonds first (each bond uses 2 electrons); complete octets of terminal atoms with lone pairs.
4Place remaining electrons on the central atom; if it still lacks an octet, convert lone pair(s) on terminal atoms into multiple bonds.
Advanced Insight — Formal Charge

When several Lewis structures are possible, the one with formal charges closest to zero (and negative formal charge on the more electronegative atom) is preferred. Formula: FC = (valence e⁻ of free atom) − (non-bonding e⁻) − ½(bonding e⁻).

Example — CO₂ vs a hypothetical O=C–O structure with one single and one triple bond: the symmetric O=C=O structure gives formal charges of 0 on C and 0 on each O, making it the correct, most stable structure. For O₃ (ozone), formal charge analysis combined with equal bond lengths confirms it must be represented as a resonance hybrid, not a single fixed structure.

NEET Exam Traps
  • Formal charge is a bookkeeping tool, not a real charge — do not confuse it with oxidation state (which assumes 100% ionic character) or the actual partial charge (from electronegativity difference).
  • Octet rule has well-known exceptions (see Section 7) — never assume every atom in a structure must have exactly 8 electrons.
  • In counting valence electrons for an ion, remember: extra electrons are ADDED for anions and REMOVED for cations — a very common sign error.

2. Ionic (Electrovalent) Bonding

An ionic bond is the electrostatic force of attraction between oppositely charged ions formed by complete transfer of one or more electrons from an electropositive atom (metal) to an electronegative atom (non-metal).

Factors favouring ionic bond formation: low ionization enthalpy of the metal, high (negative) electron gain enthalpy of the non-metal, and high lattice enthalpy of the resulting solid.

Figure 4.1: The Born–Haber cycle — five steps connecting elements in their standard states to the ionic solid, used to indirectly calculate lattice enthalpy.

By Hess's Law: ΔHf(MX) = ΔHsub + IE + ½BE + ΔegH + ΔHlattice. Since lattice enthalpy itself cannot be measured directly, it is the term usually calculated from this cycle when all other quantities are known.

Advanced Insight — What Controls Lattice Enthalpy

Lattice enthalpy ∝ (charge on cation × charge on anion) / (inter-ionic distance). So MgO (charges +2, −2, small ions) has a far higher lattice enthalpy than NaCl (charges +1, −1, larger ions) — this is why MgO has a much higher melting point than NaCl.

Fajans' Rules predict when a "mostly ionic" bond gains significant covalent character (polarisation of the anion's electron cloud by the cation): covalent character increases with (i) small, highly charged cation (high polarising power), (ii) large, highly charged anion (high polarisability), and (iii) a cation with pseudo-noble-gas / 18-electron configuration (e.g. Cu⁺, Ag⁺) rather than true noble-gas configuration, since d-electrons shield the nucleus poorly. Classic example: AlCl₃ is significantly covalent despite Al being a metal, because Al³⁺ is small and highly charged.

NEET Exam Traps
  • Lattice enthalpy is always taken as a positive quantity when defined as energy required to separate the solid into gaseous ions (endothermic); its formation from gaseous ions is exothermic (negative), so watch the sign convention used in the question.
  • LiF has anomalously low solubility in water compared to other alkali halides because its very high lattice enthalpy (small ionic sizes) is not fully compensated by hydration enthalpy.
  • Ionic compounds conduct electricity only in molten state or aqueous solution (free ions), never in the solid state, where ions are locked in a rigid lattice.

3. Bond Parameters

ParameterDefinition & Key Trend
Bond LengthEquilibrium distance between nuclei of two bonded atoms. Decreases as bond order increases (single > double > triple in length) and as atomic size decreases.
Bond AngleAngle between orbitals containing the bonding electron pairs around the central atom, measured in degrees.
Bond EnthalpyEnergy needed to break 1 mole of a particular bond in the gaseous state. Increases with bond order (triple > double > single) — hence bond enthalpy and bond length are inversely related.
Bond OrderNumber of bonds (single, double or triple) between two atoms in a molecule — e.g. 1 for N–H, 2 for O=O, 3 for N≡N. Higher bond order → shorter, stronger bond.
Dipole Moment (μ)μ = charge (Q) × distance between charge centres (r), measured in Debye (D); 1 D = 3.336 × 10⁻³⁰ C·m. A vector quantity — points from the positive to the negative end of the bond (by physics convention; older chemistry convention shows the arrow the other way).
% Ionic Character= (observed dipole moment / dipole moment for 100% ionic bond) × 100 — used to quantify how "ionic" a polar covalent bond really is.
Advanced Insight — Dipole Moment of Polyatomic Molecules

For polyatomic molecules, the net dipole moment is the vector sum of all individual bond dipoles (including lone pair contributions). This is why molecular shape directly determines polarity:

  • CO₂ (linear, symmetric) → individual C=O dipoles cancel → μ = 0, non-polar, despite polar bonds.
  • H₂O (bent) → dipoles do not cancel, and the lone pairs on O reinforce the net dipole → μ = 1.84 D, strongly polar.
  • NH₃ (pyramidal) has a higher dipole moment than NF₃ (also pyramidal) because in NH₃ the lone pair dipole and the three N–H bond dipoles point the same general way, while in NF₃ the highly electronegative F atoms pull bond dipoles opposite to the lone pair, partially cancelling it — a favourite NEET conceptual trap.
NEET Exam Traps
  • BeF₂ and BF₃ are non-polar (μ = 0) despite having polar bonds, purely due to their symmetric linear/trigonal-planar geometry — geometry, not just electronegativity difference, decides overall polarity.
  • Isoelectronic species can have different bond lengths if their bond order differs — always check bond order before comparing bond length across a series like CO, NO⁺, CN⁻, N₂.
  • A higher dipole moment does not always mean a "more ionic-looking" molecule is more reactive — dipole moment measures charge separation, not reactivity directly.

4. VSEPR Theory & Molecular Shapes

The Valence Shell Electron Pair Repulsion (VSEPR) theory (Sidgwick–Powell, extended by Nyholm–Gillespie) predicts molecular geometry by minimising repulsion between electron pairs (bonding + lone) around the central atom.

Repulsion order: lone pair–lone pair > lone pair–bond pair > bond pair–bond pair. A lone pair occupies more space (held by only one nucleus) and compresses adjacent bond angles — this is why H₂O (2 lone pairs, ~104.5°) has a smaller bond angle than NH₃ (1 lone pair, ~107°), which in turn is smaller than CH₄ (0 lone pairs, 109.5°), even though all three central atoms are roughly sp³ hybridised.
Electron pairsType (AXₙEₘ)ShapeBond AngleExample
2AX₂Linear180°BeCl₂, CO₂
3AX₃Trigonal planar120°BF₃, SO₃
3AX₂EBent / angular<120°SO₂, O₃
4AX₄Tetrahedral109.5°CH₄, SiCl₄, SO₄²⁻
4AX₃ETrigonal pyramidal~107°NH₃, PCl₃
4AX₂E₂Bent / angular~104.5°H₂O, OF₂
5AX₅Trigonal bipyramidal90° & 120°PCl₅
5AX₄ESee-saw~90°, ~120°, ~173°SF₄
5AX₃E₂T-shaped~90°ClF₃
5AX₂E₃Linear180°XeF₂, I₃⁻
6AX₆Octahedral90°SF₆
6AX₅ESquare pyramidal~90°BrF₅, XeOF₄
6AX₄E₂Square planar90°XeF₄
NEET Exam Traps
  • "Shape" (based only on positions of atoms) and "electron geometry" (based on all electron pairs including lone pairs) are different — NH₃ has tetrahedral electron geometry but pyramidal molecular shape; always read the question carefully.
  • In AX₄E and AX₃E₂ trigonal-bipyramidal-derived shapes, lone pairs always occupy equatorial positions first (less repulsion, only two 90° neighbours vs three for axial) — this decides why SF₄ is see-saw, not another geometry.
  • Multiple bonds (double/triple) behave like a single "electron domain" for VSEPR counting purposes, but exert slightly greater repulsion than a single bond pair.

5. Valence Bond Theory & Hybridisation

Valence Bond Theory (VBT) (Heitler–London, extended by Pauling & Slater) says a covalent bond forms by overlap of half-filled atomic orbitals of two atoms with opposite spins; greater overlap → stronger bond. Orbitals overlapping along the internuclear axis give a σ (sigma) bond; sidewise overlap of parallel unhybridised p-orbitals gives a π (pi) bond, which is always weaker than a σ bond in the same pair of atoms due to smaller overlap.

Hybridisation is the intermixing of atomic orbitals of slightly different energies on the same atom to give a new set of equivalent-energy hybrid orbitals, better suited for bond formation and matching observed geometry.

HybridisationOrbitals mixedGeometry% s characterExample
sp1s + 1pLinear (180°)50%BeCl₂, C₂H₂ (each C)
sp²1s + 2pTrigonal planar (120°)33.3%BF₃, C₂H₄ (each C)
sp³1s + 3pTetrahedral (109.5°)25%CH₄, NH₃, H₂O
sp³d1s + 3p + 1dTrigonal bipyramidal20%PCl₅
sp³d²1s + 3p + 2dOctahedral16.7%SF₆
sp³d³1s + 3p + 3dPentagonal bipyramidal14.3%IF₇
Advanced Insight — s-Character Controls Bond Angle & Bond Strength

A hybrid orbital with higher % s-character is held closer to the nucleus (more spherical, lower energy) — bonds formed from it are shorter and stronger, and the bond angle between two such hybrid orbitals is larger. This is why sp (50% s) > sp² (33%) > sp³ (25%) in bond angle, and why C–H bonds in ethyne (sp, 180°) are shorter and stronger than in ethene (sp², 120°), which are shorter than in ethane (sp³, 109.5°).

A common exam-level subtlety: hybridisation of a molecule with multiple bonds or lone pairs is decided by the total number of σ-bonds + lone pairs on the central atom (not by counting π-bonds). E.g. in CO₂, carbon has 2 σ-bonds and 0 lone pairs → sp hybridised, with the two π-bonds formed from unhybridised p-orbitals perpendicular to each other.

NEET Exam Traps
  • Hybridisation is a theoretical model to rationalise observed geometry — it is derived FROM the shape (via VSEPR electron-pair count), not the other way round; don't try to "predict" shape independently of counting electron domains.
  • d-orbital involvement in sp³d/sp³d² hybridisation (expanded octet) is only possible for elements from period 3 onward (has accessible d-orbitals) — never for period 2 elements like N, O, F, which is why NF₅ and OF₄ do not exist while PF₅ and SF₆ do.
  • Bond angle deviates from the "ideal" hybridisation angle whenever lone pairs or differing electronegativities of substituents are present — don't just quote the textbook angle without checking lone pairs (e.g. H₂O is sp³ but its angle is 104.5°, not 109.5°).

6. Molecular Orbital Theory (MOT)

Unlike VBT (which localises electrons in bonds), Molecular Orbital Theory (Hund–Mulliken) treats electrons as delocalised over the whole molecule. Atomic orbitals combine via Linear Combination of Atomic Orbitals (LCAO): constructive overlap gives a lower-energy bonding MO (σ, π); destructive overlap gives a higher-energy antibonding MO (σ*, π*) with a node between the nuclei.

Energy orderApplies to
σ1s < σ*1s < σ2s < σ*2s < (π2px = π2py) < σ2pz < (π*2px = π*2py) < σ*2pzLi₂, Be₂, B₂, C₂, N₂ (no/small s–p mixing effect ignored below Z ≤ 7)
σ1s < σ*1s < σ2s < σ*2s < σ2pz < (π2px = π2py) < (π*2px = π*2py) < σ*2pzO₂, F₂, Ne₂ (σ2pz drops below the π2p pair since s–p mixing is negligible here)
Bond order (BO) = ½(number of electrons in bonding MOs − number in antibonding MOs). Rules: BO > 0 → molecule can exist and is stable; higher BO → shorter bond length & higher bond enthalpy; if any MO has unpaired electrons, the species is paramagnetic (attracted into a magnetic field); if all electrons are paired, it is diamagnetic.
SpeciesTotal e⁻Bond OrderMagnetic Behaviour
H₂21Diamagnetic
He₂40 (does not exist)—
N₂143Diamagnetic
O₂162Paramagnetic (2 unpaired e⁻ in π*2p)
O₂⁺152.5Paramagnetic (bond order rises, bond strengthens vs O₂)
O₂⁻ (superoxide)171.5Paramagnetic (bond order falls vs O₂)
F₂181Diamagnetic
N₂⁺132.5Paramagnetic (bond order falls vs N₂, since electron removed from bonding σ2pz)
CO143Diamagnetic (isoelectronic with N₂)
Advanced Insight — MOT Succeeds Where Lewis Theory Fails

The single most-quoted triumph of MOT over the simple Lewis/VBT picture is O₂'s paramagnetism: the Lewis structure O=O shows all electrons paired, predicting diamagnetism, but experimentally liquid O₂ is attracted to a magnet. MOT correctly explains this because the last two electrons must singly occupy the degenerate π*2px and π*2py orbitals (Hund's rule), leaving 2 unpaired electrons.

Removing an electron from N₂ (bond order 3) to form N₂⁺ removes it from a bonding σ2pz orbital, so bond order falls to 2.5 and the bond weakens. Removing an electron from O₂ (bond order 2) to form O₂⁺ removes it from an antibonding π*2p orbital, so bond order rises to 2.5 and the bond actually strengthens — this reversal is a favourite higher-order NEET question.

NEET Exam Traps
  • Never use the O₂/F₂-type energy order (σ2pz below π2p) for N₂ or lighter diatomics — using the wrong order for N₂ wrongly predicts it to be paramagnetic.
  • Bond order can be a fraction (e.g. 1.5, 2.5) for ions — this is normal in MOT and is not an error.
  • Isoelectronic species (same total electron count) have the same bond order and similar MO filling — CO and N₂ (both 14 e⁻, BO 3) is the most-tested pair.

7. Hydrogen Bonding, Resonance & Exceptions to the Octet Rule

Hydrogen bonding is a special dipole–dipole attraction between an H atom covalently bonded to a highly electronegative, small atom (F, O, N) and a lone pair on another electronegative atom (F, O, N) nearby — weaker than covalent/ionic bonds but much stronger than ordinary van der Waals forces.

TypeDescriptionExample
Intermolecular H-bondBetween H of one molecule and electronegative atom of another; raises boiling point / melting point sharply.H₂O, HF, NH₃ — anomalously high boiling points vs. their heavier group analogues (H₂S, HCl, PH₃)
Intramolecular H-bondWithin the same molecule, forming a ring; tends to lower boiling point / water solubility vs. the intermolecular case, and can affect acidity.o-Nitrophenol, salicylaldehyde

Resonance: When a single Lewis structure cannot correctly represent a molecule/ion (e.g. bond lengths that are experimentally identical but a single structure predicts different bond orders), the actual structure is a hybrid of several contributing (canonical) structures. The real molecule is more stable than any single canonical form — this extra stabilisation is resonance energy. Classic examples: O₃, CO₃²⁻, NO₃⁻, benzene (all C–C bonds equal, intermediate between single and double).

Exceptions to the Octet Rule
  • Incomplete octet: Central atom has fewer than 8 electrons — e.g. BeCl₂ (4 e⁻ around Be), BF₃ (6 e⁻ around B), AlCl₃.
  • Odd-electron species: Total valence electrons are odd, so octet cannot be completed on every atom — e.g. NO, NO₂ (free radicals).
  • Expanded octet: Central atom (period 3 or beyond, with accessible d-orbitals) accommodates more than 8 electrons — e.g. PCl₅ (10 e⁻), SF₆ (12 e⁻), H₂SO₄, ClF₃.
Advanced Insight — Rules for Writing Resonance Structures
  • All canonical structures must have the same atomic positions/connectivity — only the arrangement of electrons (lone pairs and π-bonds) differs.
  • All contributing structures should have roughly the same energy (comparable stability) to contribute significantly; a structure with unfavourable formal charges (e.g. positive charge on the more electronegative atom) contributes less.
  • The actual molecule is NOT rapidly "flipping" between structures — it is a single, time-independent hybrid with bond lengths/orders intermediate between the contributing forms (e.g. each C–O bond in CO₃²⁻ has a bond order of 4/3, not alternating between 1 and 2).
NEET Exam Traps
  • Do not equate resonance with tautomerism — resonance structures differ only in electron placement (same atoms, same connectivity, interconverting only "on paper"); tautomers are genuinely different, interconvertible molecules with atoms/bonds actually moving.
  • H-bonding requires H attached to F, O or N specifically — a C–H bond practically never forms a significant hydrogen bond (C is not electronegative enough) except in rare, weak cases.
  • HF has a lower boiling point than water despite stronger individual H-bonds, because each HF molecule can form only 2 H-bonds (linear, chain-like network) vs. water's 4 (extensive 3-D tetrahedral network) — bond strength alone does not decide boiling point; network connectivity matters too.
